title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: The certificate says Award of Merit. It gives the year, 1939, and the recipient’s name, and it names the event: a Gas Model Hydroplane Meet, held in connection with the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island. The printed formula around the blanks calls him an outstanding junior citizen. It carries two signatures, one of them Leland W. Cutler’s, president of the exposition.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: That is the whole of the document. It is the earliest object in the collection that has anything to do with the way things move.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: Frank Calicura turned eighteen six weeks after the fair opened. He was the son of an Italian mule skinner and blacksmith, one of seventeen children in a house on Mellus Street in Martinez, thirty miles northeast across the water, and he cut meat for a living in his older brother’s shop. What he had built was a boat designed not to displace water but to escape it — a hydroplane rides on top of the surface once it is moving fast enough to break the grip of it. Adults judged it and found it worth a certificate.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: The ground he stood on to collect it had not existed four years earlier.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: In February 1936 the Army Corps of Engineers began dumping rock and sand onto the shoals north of Yerba Buena Island. More than nineteen million cubic yards came off the bottom of the bay, topped with barged-in soil, until there were four hundred flat acres in the middle of San Francisco Bay where there had been open water. They called it Treasure Island, after the gold that might be in the fill.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: The fair was the interim use. The island had been built to be an airport.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: Federal money paid for the dredging and for three permanent structures — a terminal building and two hangars along the south shore — intended to serve San Francisco’s municipal airport once the exposition closed. The north end, where the runways were to go, was paved for the time being as parking for twelve thousand cars.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: Pan American Airways moved its flying-boat operation over from Alameda on January 23, 1939, three weeks before the gates opened. The Clippers came down in the cove alongside the fairground. Pan Am was itself an exhibit: one of the hangars was fitted with a spectators’ gallery so that fairgoers could stand and watch mechanics overhaul transpacific aircraft.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: Ten million people came in 1939, and five million more the following summer. The fair celebrated two finished bridges and the ascendancy of California in the Pacific.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: The airport was never built. The Navy took the island in 1941 and held it for fifty-six years. The Clippers were out of regular service by the end of the war, and San Francisco built its airport south of the city instead, on the tidal flats at Mills Field.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: So the certificate records a butcher’s son from a refinery town, judged competent at a small problem in moving water, on an artificial island built to be an airfield, at a fair about the Pacific Ocean, twenty-eight months before the Navy took the ground and the ocean became something else entirely.

title: The Award of Merit
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines The Award of Merit
body: It does not say he wanted to fly. Nothing in the record says that yet.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: The house at 515 Mellus Street belonged to Sam and Angelina Calicura, and it held seventeen children.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: The number is the first fact of Frank Calicura’s life, and it is an economic fact before it is a sentimental one. A household that size in an immigrant town during the Depression is a labor pool with a rotation of wages coming into it — the older ones working, the middle ones minding the younger ones, everything pooled against one roof. It also means that a boy born in 1921 grows up under several men who function as his fathers.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: Seventeen is the family’s own number, and this book keeps it. The paper supports sixteen. The Gazette counted a sixteenth birth in August 1928, and no birth after it is documented anywhere in the collection. The seventeenth is carried here on the family’s authority alone, and remains unaccounted for.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: Seventeen is also the first in a long series. Almost everything that can be established about Frank Calicura now arrives as a figure someone had a reason to write down — hours logged, a score on a scale of one to nine, the size of a crew, the count of missions flown. The family kept the objects. The institutions kept the numbers. Both are in the record, and they do not always agree.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: The eldest had been born in Italy in 1906, fifteen years ahead of Frank. The father had come over as Saverio Colacurcio, and the eldest son carried the same first name — a second Saverio, differing from his father only in the middle — and there were two Sams in the house, because Americans called them both that.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: The surname did not survive the school system. A name-change document in the family’s collection records the family becoming Calicura, and the account attached to it gives the reason: around 1914 the eldest son was failing at school, and the Martinez school district suggested a spelling that teachers and clerks could manage. He was eight. Saverio Colacurcio had carried the name he was born with through Ellis Island in 1902, through the Pennsylvania coal towns, and across the country to a refinery on the Carquinez Strait. It came off in a classroom.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: In print afterward the father is Sam Calicura and the son Sam Calicura Jr., though the two men did not share a middle name and so were never strictly Senior and Junior; the papers were solving the same problem the household had, in the same rough way. The change also dates the record. A Colacurcio in a Martinez newspaper belongs to the years before 1914. A Calicura belongs to the years after.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: The name was worth managing. On May 29, 1940, the Martinez News-Gazette ran a notice he had bought, on page 2, under the heading TO MY FRIENDS and signed by the eldest son: word had reached him that someone named Calicura had been arrested, and people had been asking whether it was him. He had never been arrested for anything, he wrote, and he had gone through the records of the city and the county himself and found no one of that name who had been. The notice does not identify the other Calicura, or explain what prompted the rumor.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: The date is worth holding onto. In 1940 the name was twenty-six years old — no longer new, but not old either, and by then attached to a butcher shop, a union local, and, that same year, a hangar going up on the waterfront fill. The man who paid for the notice was thirty-four and in the middle of building his town an airport. What it shows is someone who understood that in a place this size a surname in print was a business asset, and that a name his family had taken at a school district’s suggestion could still be damaged by a stranger who happened to carry it.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: Martinez had been the seat of Contra Costa County since 1850, on the south shore of the Carquinez Strait where the rivers come down to meet the bay. Portuguese and Italian fishermen had worked that water since the 1870s, productively enough that by 1882 two of the twelve fishing canneries on the Pacific Coast were operating there, shipping salmon to Europe, the eastern states, Australia, New Zealand, and Hawaii. Commercial fishing supported families in the town until the bay was closed to it in 1957. Italians settled the place heavily in the last quarter of the century and started a wine industry that later moved to the Napa Valley. Joe DiMaggio was born there in 1914, to a fishing family, and the town has never once stopped mentioning it.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: Then the oil came, because the harbor was deep and the railroad already ran along the waterfront. Shell built its refinery on the Martinez shore in 1915. Associated Oil put another three miles away a few years after. By the time Frank was old enough to work, the town ran on two economies at once — the old one that came out of the water, and the new one that came off the hill in a smell you could navigate by.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: Frank finished at Alhambra High in 1938 and went to cut meat for his brother at the Star Meat Market on Main Street. The family had been in the meat business since about 1925.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: He also left the house that year. From 1938 his address is 731 Mellus Street, a few blocks from the one he was raised in — the address that would appear on his enlistment papers, on the envelope carrying news of his son’s birth to Florida in 1944, and on his medical certificate as a civil airman four years after the war. He was seventeen. The house of seventeen children is the house he grew up in, not the one he lived in as an adult; he was gone from it before he was old enough to enlist.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: His 1938 Alhambra High yearbook entry survives in the collection, and it is the earliest piece of Frank Calicura's own world on record — not a document about him, but his classmates' shorthand for who he already was. It notes him “seen delivering for his brother,” his ambition given as wanting “to swing a bat,” and his likely destiny, in the yearbook's own joke, as “swinging hash.” The prophecy was not far off. He stayed in the meat trade, on and off, for the rest of his working life.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: Butchering in 1938 was a trade, not a job. It carried an apprenticeship, a union card, and a body of knowledge that took years to get into the hands: where a joint will part on its own, what a bone tells you through a blade, how to hold a knife so the work lasts a full day. Men were paid for knowing it and they defended what they were paid.

title: Seventeen
titleText: The Weight of Small Machines Seventeen
body: That is what he did from 1938 until the Army finally sent for him: cutting meat on Main Street for his brother, in a town of seven thousand people that smelled of oil and salt water.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The ground had a history before Beatie and Calicura ever touched it. The Gazette had floated the idea of a municipal airport on the Martinez waterfront as early as August 1927, and by January 1928 the paper was proposing the same reclaimed ground east of the municipal wharf that the airfield would eventually occupy. A deputy sheriff built the first hangar there in 1933. The field opened, in some rough working form, in July 1935 — though by one account its condition was not the best. It was still too minor to appear on any aeronautical chart as late as 1936; the earliest surviving photograph of it dates to 1937, showing a single runway and a few small buildings on the west side.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: So in 1939, when two men who owned airplanes and had nowhere in Martinez to keep them turned their attention to that ground, they were not starting from nothing. They were taking over a strip that had already sat there, half-working, for six years, and beginning to rebuild it into something a city would grant exclusive commercial rights to operate.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: Charles Beatie lived in Pleasant Hill. Sam Calicura Jr. lived in Martinez and was Frank’s eldest brother. Both kept their aircraft at other people’s fields because Martinez had no hangar. The land they chose belonged to the city and had been made, not found — filled ground along the strait, level and worthless and adjacent to the Southern Pacific line that ran the length of the waterfront.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The Tribune of July 24 carried it: Martinez Aviators Begin Work Of Restoring City’s Flying Field. Charles Beattie and Sam Calicura, owners of planes housed elsewhere for lack of hangars, discing and dragging a runway on filled land belonging to the city. Moral support, no money. Waterfront Commissioner C. A. Ricks would not object to hangars and would not build them. The paper spells Beattie with two t’s.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: Sam Calicura Jr. appears in the family’s photographs the way he appears in its history — present, central, and rarely the subject. One portrait from the early 1940s shows him with his son Richard, born in 1934, both of them in suits and ties.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The city gave them what the record calls moral support and no money at all. What it did give was introductions. The waterfront commissioner, C. A. Ricks, and the council offered their good offices with Pacific Gas and Electric and with Shell Oil, whose refinery stood above the town, for whatever accommodations an airstrip on that ground was going to need.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: This is how most small American airfields came into existence in the late 1930s. Not through appropriation or federal program, but through two or three men with airplanes, a piece of ground nobody wanted, and a municipality willing to be helpful in every way that did not involve a check.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: By 1940 Ricks had been elected mayor, and Beatie and Calicura had come away from a meeting with him holding exclusive rights to operate a commercial airport on the Martinez waterfront.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The meeting was covered directly. On December 12, 1940, Sam Calicura and Beatie appeared before the city council to ask terms for leasing hangar space on the waterfront, telling councilmen they held a deposit on a building at the San Francisco World's Fair and needed to move it off Treasure Island as soon as possible. They asked for the exclusive right to operate a commercial hangar on the field. Mayor Ricks told the council that since the two men were “pioneering the situation,” he felt they were entitled to protection and should have “first crack at everything as long as they are doing right.” The council agreed, verbally, to grant the lease.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The Golden Gate International Exposition was closing, and that was the whole of their hurry. The Gazette says only this much about what they bought: a building, purchased at the exposition grounds, for airplane hangar purposes. It does not say which building, or what it had been used for during the fair, and nothing else in the collection does either. It came in pieces, by truck, across the bridge and down to the strait, and the work ran late through a wet winter. The power lines strung around the field were a problem the whole time; with a hangar added to the ground beneath them, the authorities judged the approach dangerous.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: A contemporary clipping dates the start precisely. In the Gazette of December 16, 1940, contractor William E. Douglas “began Saturday” — the fourteenth — erecting the building on the airport grounds; the structure, the paper noted, would house several planes. Beatie had purchased a new 105, a three-place cabin Stinson, for the field.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: So: the fair Frank Calicura had visited in 1939, on an island dredged out of the bay to be an airport that was never built, was dismantled — and one of its buildings was trucked to Martinez and stood up on filled land beside the railroad tracks, where it became the hangar of an airport that actually existed.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: Which building it had been is worth wanting to know and not worth guessing at. Treasure Island had been laid out with a terminal and two hangars along its south shore, built for the municipal airport it was supposed to become; it also had the Gayway, and exhibition halls, and a great deal else. Any of it was for sale that winter. The Gazette reported a purchase, not a provenance.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The hangar's completion did not end the field's troubles. A Gazette clipping dated February 27, 1941 quotes Sam Calicura Jr. directly on the problem that had dogged the site from the start: hazardous wires on the airport's east side, he said, were the one factor keeping a shop operator from locating there, and their removal would let two developments follow — a representative of the Franklin Aircraft Corporation had already asked about installing a motor repair shop next to the hangar, and the Twin-Coach Company, which operated a fleet of delivery trucks and kept two planes for taxiing its own personnel, was prepared to base its aircraft at the field permanently once the wires came down. The hangar itself, once finished, would measure 65 by 75 feet — large enough for eight to ten medium-size ships — and most of that space, Calicura said, was already spoken for.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: Some of that promised traffic arrived. An undated clipping in the collection reports that Warren Susan of the Alameda Air Service had reached an agreement with Sam Calicura and Beatie, by then established as lessees of the field, to move his servicing operation to Martinez — five employees relocating with it, and Susan himself erecting a shop at the airport hangar. Susan was, at the time, rebuilding an eight-place Travelair-6000 seaplane, which he intended to base and operate from Martinez once the move was complete, alongside service work he already performed for other operators in the area. The field that had opened as two men's private ambition was, within a year, drawing outside business to the waterfront on its own account.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: A hand-drawn plan of the finished field survives in the collection, undated and unsigned, titled Martinez Airpark and drawn to a scale of one inch to two hundred feet. It gives the runway as 2,112 feet by 100, with a second strip of 1,800 by 50 running off it at an angle, a parking area, taxi strips, a road along the south edge, and a single building 60 by 70 feet.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: Most of the sheet is not about dimensions. It is about oil. The entire runway was to be oiled lightly, to lay dust; the center fifty feet oiled heavy, to withstand water; the taxi strips oiled heavy and crowned eight inches; the parking area oiled for dust only; the road oiled heavy. Five specifications, all addressing the same fact — that the field was made ground on a strait, and what it mostly had to survive was weather.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The building on the plan is 60 by 70 feet. The Gazette, quoting Sam Calicura Jr. in February 1941, gave the hangar as 65 by 75. The plan is undated, and the difference may be nothing more than the gap between a figure quoted to a reporter and a figure measured afterward, but the two are not the same and this book does not reconcile them.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: Sam Calicura Jr. was the field’s co-founder and its vice president. He taught his two younger brothers to fly there. A group plate from the strip shows him fourth from the left, in a suit, no cap. The other men are not named here.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: That last sentence is the one to read slowly. Frank Calicura did not go looking for aviation, did not answer a recruiting poster, and did not have a moment of vocation that anyone recorded. His older brother rebuilt an airfield four blocks from the family’s front door and taught him, and taught Dominic, on that strip of fill between the refinery and the water.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: Both of them enlisted as Aviation Cadets in June 1942.

title: The Fill
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Fill
body: The short snorter dollar bill in the family’s collection carries the signatures of men and women connected to that airport. Charles Beatie’s name is on it.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: In July 1942 a national aviation magazine ran a section on the Metropolitan Oakland unit of the Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association. Two of the men in it were Charles Beatie and Sam Calicura Jr., photographed with a Curtiss Robin.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: They were the same two men who had rebuilt a runway on the Martinez waterfront three years earlier. What had happened to that airport in the interval is the reason the photograph exists.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: Late in that interval, and before the war closed it off, the same association ran a competition flight over Alameda County. Pilots were handed photographs of ground objectives, sent up to locate them and mark them on a flight map, and asked to predict their own flying time before takeoff; air raid warning lookouts tracked the aircraft from the ground and reported what they saw. The winner was Sam Calicura of Martinez. He spotted every objective on his route and judged his own flying time to within fifteen seconds. Charles Beatie, flying the same exercise, was thirty seconds off. The clipping carries no date, but a Junior Chamber of Commerce Aviation Day and an association meeting set for October 28 place it in the autumn of 1941 — a matter of weeks, as it turned out, before the thing being rehearsed for arrived and the rehearsing stopped.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: On December 8, 1941, every civil aircraft in the United States except the airliners was grounded. The ban was lifted two days later for most of the country. It was not lifted for the West Coast. Restrictions on private flying along the coast continued after that, in a region the government had decided was the likeliest to be attacked next — and Martinez sits on a strait with a Shell refinery above it, twenty-five miles from the Golden Gate.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: So the field that two private owners had rebuilt out of city fill, a bought fairground building, and their own labor was closed to the flying it existed for, within eleven months of receiving its operating rights.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: Grounded did not mean idle. The Gazette reported it on December 12, 1941, five days after Pearl Harbor and four after the grounding: a Contra Costa County sheriff’s air posse, fully organized, M. V. Hanley of El Cerrito elected president, Ed McLaughlin of Albany secretary, with Sam Calicura and Charlie Beatie of Martinez named to its organizing committee alongside members drawn from across the county. The unit had, by its own account, no aircraft currently permitted to fly. It organized anyway, on the working assumption that the restrictions would eventually lift and that trained pilots would be worth having ready for defense work when they did. That is the same reasoning the Civil Air Patrol would formalize nationally within months. Here it shows up first as a county sheriff’s volunteer roster, assembled by men with nothing to fly, before Washington caught up to the idea.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: The Metropolitan Oakland unit put that principle into practice directly. An AOPA national bulletin praised the group by name for keeping flying activity alive on a grounded coast, citing a successful overnight excursion to Quincy via the Western Pacific Railroad and a Memorial Day weekend trip to Reno, held over the last weekend of May. Beatie and Calicura, pictured beside their Curtiss Robin, were named as the unit's flight chairman and vice president. The bulletin invited any pilot in a grounded area of the western defense region to write the unit's secretary in Berkeley for details on running a similar program. What circulated nationally was the Oakland unit's answer to being grounded, not Martinez — but two of the men answering for it were the two who had rebuilt the Martinez runway out of the fill.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: The organization that absorbed men in this position had been created six days before Pearl Harbor. On December 1, 1941, Fiorello LaGuardia, running the Office of Civilian Defense, signed the order establishing the Civil Air Patrol, with Maj. Gen. John F. Curry as its first national commander. Its founders had spent two years arguing that the country’s private pilots and their aircraft were a national asset that would otherwise be grounded and wasted. Within a month of its creation they were proved right in the most direct way available.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: The Curtiss Robin in the photograph was a fourteen-year-old airplane. It first flew in 1928, a high-wing cabin monoplane from the era when a manufacturer still expected to sell aircraft to private citizens the way one sold automobiles. By 1942 it was thoroughly obsolete and thoroughly useful — an airframe that could carry a man aloft to look at something and bring him back.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: Sam Calicura Jr. was thirty-six that summer. He was past the age ceiling for aviation cadet training by a decade, he had been born in Italy, and he had a business. He was not going to fly a bomber. What he did instead was teach — young flyers, through the Civil Air Patrol, which is what he had already been doing at Martinez without a war to justify it.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: His name and his photograph were in a national magazine in July 1942.

title: Flying, July 1942
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks Flying, July 1942
body: His two younger brothers had enlisted as Aviation Cadets the month before.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: The *Contra Costa Gazette* recorded it in June 1942: two of the Calicura brothers, Frank and Dominic, had enlisted as Aviation Cadets.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: The clipping the family kept does not treat them as a pair. Under the heading CONTRA COSTA IN THE WAR, Dominic F. Calicura, of 515 Mellus Street, has been accepted by the Mather Field Cadet Examining Board and will be sent to Santa Ana for pre-flight. Frank, employed with his eldest brother Sam at the Star Meat Market, is standing by, expecting notice momentarily for similar duty. Both Alhambra High. Joyce remaining in Martinez, employed with the Pacific Telephone and Telegraph Company. The paper does not date the column. This book has both men enlisting in June 1942. The clipping is the hometown version of that month: one brother already accepted, the other still at the block.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: Six months earlier Frank would not have qualified. Until January 1942 the Army required two years of college of anyone entering aviation cadet training, and he had none — he had finished high school in 1938 and gone to work cutting meat. Then on January 15, 1942 the requirement was struck out and replaced with an examination. The Aviation Cadet Qualifying Examination measured what the college requirement had been standing in for, and measured it better; college men now sat the same test as everyone else. The doorway that opened for Frank Calicura opened because the Army had finally worked out that a transcript was a poor instrument.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: What he enlisted into was not the Army, exactly. It was a waiting room.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: The Air Corps Enlisted Reserve had been established in April 1942 for precisely this purpose. A qualified applicant could enlist for active duty as an unassigned private and go sit on a base — or he could enlist in the reserve, go home, keep his civilian job, and wait to be called when a training slot opened. The Air Corps wanted the men claimed and on its books. It did not yet have anywhere to put them.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: So Frank Calicura, aviation cadet, spent the second half of 1942 cutting meat on Main Street for his brother.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: He was not alone in it. By December 1942 roughly ninety-three thousand men were in the same condition — enlisted, classified as future aircrew, and waiting. Many had been waiting six or seven months. The pool was large enough and idle enough that the selective service boards and the War Manpower Commission began asking about it, and the Air Corps’ own reasoning for holding them was recorded without embarrassment: better to store the men and risk a morale problem than release them and let the public conclude that the Air Corps had more cadets than it could use.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: The bottleneck was never volunteers. After Pearl Harbor there were more than the system could absorb. What the Army lacked was instructors, airfields, and aircraft, and the entire enormous training apparatus of 1943 was built to work through a backlog that already existed before it opened.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: The solution arrived in January 1943, when the Secretary of War ordered the reserve called up and sent to college. About a hundred institutions were selected to begin with. The official history of the Army Air Forces is unusually blunt about why: the college program came into being not to meet an educational need but to hold a backlog of aircrew candidates. At its height in April 1943 more than sixty thousand men were in college training detachments at over a hundred and fifty schools.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: Frank was called in February 1943 and sent to Houghton, Michigan, on the Keweenaw Peninsula, five hundred miles north of Chicago, to study physics and mathematics in a winter he had no preparation for.

title: The Reserve
titleText: The Strip by the Tracks The Reserve
body: What the record gives of those eight months is the work and the length of them. Nothing else.

title: The Iron Country
titleText: The Locked Door The Iron Country
body: The Keweenaw Peninsula runs northeast into Lake Superior like a spur bolted onto the rest of Michigan, and it had been ground zero for America’s first mineral rush a full generation before California ever had one — copper, not gold, pulled out of the rock there from the 1840s forward. By 1943 the boom was decades gone, but the town it had built was still standing: Houghton, home to the Michigan College of Mining and Technology, a mining school in a mining town, closer to the Canadian border than to anywhere Frank Calicura had ever lived.

title: The Iron Country
titleText: The Locked Door The Iron Country
body: The reason a mining college a thousand miles from any ocean ended up training Army Air Forces cadets had nothing to do with geography and everything to do with real estate. The college had classrooms sitting mostly empty in wartime, a physical plant the government could lease at a fraction of what building new barracks would cost, and a faculty that already knew how to teach physics and engineering mathematics to young men. The same arithmetic was applied to more than a hundred colleges across the country in 1943 — a national College Training Detachment program stitched together out of whatever campus space the war hadn’t already claimed for something else.

title: The Iron Country
titleText: The Locked Door The Iron Country
body: Frank had spent his whole life at sea level, in a refinery town on tidal water three thousand miles away. Houghton put him somewhere the harbor froze over by December and stayed that way past Easter. The distance was the whole point of how the Army was running this war: move men to wherever there was room, not wherever made any particular sense for the man being moved.

title: The Books on the Table
titleText: The Locked Door The Books on the Table
body: What the Army handed him at Houghton was a stack of textbooks and a schedule that left no room to fall behind on any of them.

title: The Books on the Table
titleText: The Locked Door The Books on the Table
body: The College Training Detachment curriculum combined sustained physical conditioning with a full academic course load — physics, mathematics through trigonometry, English, geography, history, and the first pieces of material a future pilot would eventually need: the basics of aerodynamics, the first vocabulary of navigation. It was compressed hard, months of instruction squeezed into weeks, and it was never really an education in the ordinary sense. It was a filter with a syllabus. The Army Air Forces used the coursework itself to find out, cheaply and in bulk, which men could actually absorb technical material under pressure — before committing a single hour of increasingly scarce flight time and increasingly scarce aircraft to any of them.

title: The Books on the Table
titleText: The Locked Door The Books on the Table
body: The physical side ran alongside it without a break in the schedule: calisthenics, obstacle courses, close-order drill on a quad packed hard with Michigan snow, the whole apparatus of making a body more disciplined running in parallel with the work of making a mind sharper. The Army was testing not only what a man knew but whether he could still function — think clearly, follow instructions, hold a formation — after being run into the ground first.

title: The Books on the Table
titleText: The Locked Door The Books on the Table
body: Frank Calicura had spent five years learning a trade with his hands, reading the edge of a knife and the balance of a scale, work that lived in the fingers as much as anywhere else. Houghton handed him bound textbooks instead and expected the same discipline to transfer. It was not obvious to him, in February 1943, that it would. Whether it did was exactly what the next several weeks were built to find out.

title: The Screening
titleText: The Locked Door The Screening
body: What Houghton did not do was decide what kind of flyer Frank Calicura was going to be.

title: The Screening
titleText: The Locked Door The Screening
body: The College Training Detachment performed academic and physical screening only. The coursework and the conditioning existed to identify who could absorb technical material and still function under sustained pressure — men who could not keep up were identified and redirected before the Army sank any further resources into training them. The actual sorting mechanism — the battery of tests that would assign a man to pilot, navigator, or bombardier training — was administered somewhere else entirely. Houghton was upstream of that decision, not the site of it.

title: The Screening
titleText: The Locked Door The Screening
body: No document in the family’s collection records Frank’s specific academic standing or physical test results from this stretch. What survives instead is smaller and more human: a yearbook from the period, carrying a short note written home, homesick for Martinez and for Joyce, that almost certainly dates to this exact winter. It is the only artifact this chapter can point to directly. Everything around it rests on the documented general function of the College Training Detachment program rather than on paper specific to Frank Calicura.

title: The Screening
titleText: The Locked Door The Screening
body: He had, by this point, already logged something like seventy-five hours in a Piper Cub back at the small strip his own brother had helped build on the Martinez waterfront — real hours, in a real cockpit, flown before the Army had any claim on him at all. None of it exempted him from anything waiting ahead. Houghton was measuring a different set of capacities than a logbook could show, and at the end of the program, Frank Calicura remained exactly what he had been at the start of it: undesignated.

title: Forwarded
titleText: The Locked Door Forwarded
body: He had not been told, because nothing at Houghton was built to tell him, whether he would fly a heavy bomber, navigate one, or aim what it carried. The men who failed the academic or physical standard at this stage were reassigned elsewhere in the Army Air Forces; the men who passed, like Frank, were simply moved forward, one stage closer to a decision the system had not yet made about them. Months of feeding, housing, and instructing a cadet was not an investment the Army abandoned easily. It sorted men in stages instead.

title: Forwarded
titleText: The Locked Door Forwarded
body: Houghton could clear a man. It could not tell him what he had been cleared for.

title: Forwarded
titleText: The Locked Door Forwarded
body: Frank left the mining college that spring with a train ticket and nothing else settled. What he was actually going to be — the word that would define the rest of his war — was still several weeks and an unrecorded train journey away, waiting in a room he had not yet walked into.

title: The Battery
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Battery
body: Frank Calicura left Houghton still undesignated.

title: The Battery
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Battery
body: No collection document records the trip, the orders, the date, or the place. What survives is the outcome, not the address. By the spring of 1943 the Army Air Forces ran classification through three centers nationwide, and a man who had come through a College Training Detachment reported to one of them still unsorted, whatever he believed about himself. Which of the three tested Frank Calicura, the collection does not say, and no attempt is made here to assign him to one on the strength of geography alone.

title: The Battery
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Battery
body: The battery itself combined a written aptitude examination with a series of psychomotor tests — coordination, reaction time, judgment under a clock — and a physical. The results were converted into a single number, the stanine, on a scale of one to nine. The number, not the man’s preference, decided the track: pilot, navigator, or bombardier.

title: The Battery
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Battery
body: The reasoning behind concentrating this work at three sites, rather than distributing it more widely, was consistency. A stanine score needed to mean the same thing in Tennessee as it meant in California, and that required identical instruments and identical conditions everywhere the test was given. The Army Air Forces had built, in effect, a single national sorting mechanism and run it through three doors.

title: The Battery
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Battery
body: Frank’s file by this point carried roughly seventy-five hours already logged in a sixty-five horsepower Piper Cub, flown over a strip his own brother had helped build on the Martinez waterfront. The hours were noted. They did not exempt him from the battery, and nothing in the record suggests the examiners weighted them. When the number came back, it said pilot — on the strength of a battery of tests, not a logbook carried from California.

title: Ten Weeks
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Ten Weeks
body: Preflight followed classification, and for Frank Calicura it happened at Maxwell Field — a preflight school by this point in the war, whatever else it had been earlier.

title: Ten Weeks
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Ten Weeks
body: The course ran roughly ten weeks, and it put no cadet near an aircraft. Half of it was classroom instruction — military law and customs, the theory of flight, the fundamentals of navigation, Morse code, aircraft recognition. The other half was physical: close-order drill, weapons familiarization with sidearm and carbine, conditioning. A cadet left preflight with no additional flight hours and a great deal more discipline than he had arrived with. The airplane itself still lay ahead.

title: Ten Weeks
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Ten Weeks
body: A class yearbook for 44-D survives from this stretch, distinct from the Bainbridge class book cited later in this chapter, and Frank's own hand is on it. Above a photograph of cadets tumbling off a train with their bags, he wrote "Welcome to Maxwell (Nuts)." Above a later photograph of the same men waving from a departing train, he wrote "Farewell to Maxwell (Thank God)." Between the two, the yearbook's own printed text describes the arrival — a haircut captioned "T.S. mister!," a retreat formation, cadets doubling across the parade ground — and the eventual transition to advanced training, where a cadet is treated as a pilot for the first time and the instructors as flight commanders rather than tormentors. The yearbook’s printed text is stock class-book copy. His two captions are not. The cover is dated September 1943: Preflight, Class of 44-D, Maxwell Field, Alabama, Vol. 3 No. 9, Paragon Press, Montgomery.

title: Ten Weeks
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Ten Weeks
body: A photograph from the same field survives: four cadets on a gun in front of a columned building. The family keeps it as Frank’s Maxwell. The other three are not named here.

title: Ten Weeks
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Ten Weeks
body: It was at some point in this stretch — the collection dates it only to 1943, Montgomery, Alabama — that Joyce crossed the country to see him. A ten-week course fixed to one post made the visit possible in a way a moving assignment would not have; there was an address to write to and a reasonable chance he would still be at it by the time a train got her there. Wartime rail travel for a civilian visiting a serviceman was not a simple undertaking — connections, cost, and a weekend’s leave on his end were all that could be counted on, and none of it was guaranteed in advance.

title: Ten Weeks
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Ten Weeks
body: A letter survives from the same visit, written in Frank’s own hand on a blank page inside the 44-D yearbook. “Darling,” it begins. “This will remind you of the most wonderful time we had together while you were here. I’m on my way to those wings and nothing can stop me now. My love for you increases each day and I’ll look forward ’till we meet again. All my love, Frankie.” (family collection). It is the first piece of Frank Calicura’s own private voice this book has been able to quote directly.

title: Ten Weeks
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Ten Weeks
body: A Kodachrome slide survives from the visit — color film, 1943, a small and by then increasingly rare extravagance. The collection’s own note ties it to what came nine months later: a son. It is worth stating once, plainly, and leaving there. The photograph is already doing what it needs to do. A second Kodachrome from the same trees names the other man Red Carpenter. The book has no other paper on him.

title: The Solo
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Solo
body: From Montgomery, a classified and preflight-trained cadet moved on to primary — the first stage that put him in an aircraft at all.

title: The Solo
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Solo
body: The certificate itself resolves what earlier research could not. Frank Calicura soloed on October 19, 1943, at Canal Field, Ocala, Florida, signed off by his instructor, Ellis G. Ort. The field had been findable all along under a name the research was not yet using. A separate certificate, issued at Ocala, names the school outright: Greenville Aviation School, a civilian flight contractor to the United States Army Air Forces, certifies that Aviation Cadet Frank James Calicura successfully completed the Primary Training Course conducted by the school under the direction of the Army Air Forces Southeast Training Center — signed by E. G. Cooper, Major, Air Corps, Army Air Forces Supervisor; Frank A. Hanley, General Manager; and A. L. Clemons, Flight Director, Commanding (family collection). It was one node in a regional system that ran the same way at every field in it. The Southeast Training Center ran its primary instruction through civilian contract schools — Carlstrom Field and Dorr Field near Arcadia, others at Lakeland, Albany, Americus, Tuscaloosa, Camden — staffed by civilian instructors under military oversight, and flying almost universally the Boeing-built Stearman PT-17, an open-cockpit biplane that had become the standard primary trainer for cadets passing through Maxwell.

title: The Solo
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Solo
body: One name on that certificate deserves a direct address, the same way this book handles other coincidental numbers and names it comes across: Greenville Aviation School’s own General Manager signed himself Frank A. Hanley — a different man entirely from Major General Hanley, who would sign Frank Calicura’s commissioning letter at Maxwell Field seven months later. Same surname, two unrelated men, at two different institutions, in two different states.

title: The Solo
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Solo
body: The course ran roughly nine or ten weeks and about sixty hours, split between dual instruction and solo flying. A cadet’s first solo — the moment an instructor climbed out of the rear cockpit and did not climb back in — was by every surviving account from the period the single most remembered event of primary training, more so than graduation itself.

title: The Solo
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Solo
body: The certificate marking Frank’s is a cartoon. Woody Woodpecker, not an eagle or a colonel’s signature. The Army let the occasion be what it was: one afternoon, one young man alone in an airplane for the first time, and paperwork that did not pretend to more gravity than the moment actually carried.

title: The Solo
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South The Solo
body: If the aircraft under Ellis Ort’s instruction was a Stearman, as the regional pattern makes likely, it was the same type — a Boeing product, the same basic biplane lineage — that Frank had already flown as a civilian at his brother’s field in Martinez. The Army’s airplane and his brother’s airplane would have differed mainly in paint.

title: What the Cub Didn’t Count
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South What the Cub Didn’t Count
body: Set side by side, the two records make an odd pair.

title: What the Cub Didn’t Count
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South What the Cub Didn’t Count
body: Seventy-five hours in a Cub at Martinez, flown before the Army had any claim on him, counted toward nothing on his classification file. A stanine score, produced in a testing room in Montgomery over the course of a single sitting, decided that he would fly. The system did not ask what his hands already knew. It asked what a battery of standardized instruments could measure about him in an afternoon, and it built his entire subsequent war on the answer.

title: What the Cub Didn’t Count
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South What the Cub Didn’t Count
body: Whether the seventy-five hours mattered anyway is not a question the record can settle. Primary training assumed no prior experience and taught as though a cadet had none. But a hand already familiar with a stick and rudder, however the Army chose to score it, is not nothing, whatever the paperwork says about where a man’s competence is supposed to have come from.

title: What the Cub Didn’t Count
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South What the Cub Didn’t Count
body: By the end of summer 1943, Frank Calicura had been tested at a classification center, drilled at Maxwell, and soloed in Florida. He held a designation the Army had chosen for him in a room he could not have located on a map two years earlier, and a certificate with a cartoon woodpecker on it. He did not yet have an airplane larger than a trainer, a crew, or any indication that most of what followed would happen four thousand miles from either Martinez or Montgomery, over a country he had not yet been told the name of.

title: 2nd Command
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South 2nd Command
body: Before Bainbridge, there was a smaller command a rung down.

title: 2nd Command
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South 2nd Command
body: A cadet leadership form from the Army Air Forces Eastern Flying Training Command, issued at Ocala, Florida, appoints Aviation Cadet Frank J. Calicura “2nd Command” of the 57th A.A.F.F.T.D., to rank as such from November 3, 1943, and dated at Ocala December 3, 1943 — signed by Emil Monsour, Captain, Air Corps, Commandant of Aviation Cadets (family collection). The two dates bracket exactly the window a separate service record gives for Frank’s primary training at Ocala: November 3 to December 3, 1943.

title: 2nd Command
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South 2nd Command
body: What the appointment does not resolve is a date already sitting uneasily in this book’s own record. The solo certificate cited in §4.3 places Frank’s first solo flight, at Canal Field, Ocala, on October 19, 1943 — more than two weeks before this appointment’s own effective date, and before the primary training window a separate service record assigns to Ocala at all. The gap is left as it stands.

title: Basic
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Basic
body: From primary, Frank Calicura moved on to basic training at Bainbridge Army Air Field in southwest Georgia, the next rung of the Southeast Training Center's ladder — a heavier, faster aircraft than the Stearman, and the first stage of instruction the Army trusted enough to hand a portion of its own discipline to the cadets themselves. On December 11, 1943, on the recommendation of his tactical officer, Aviation Cadet Frank J. Calicura was appointed Flight Sergeant of the Aviation Cadet Basic Training Group at Bainbridge — put in a limited chain of command over other cadets before he had finished training himself.

title: Basic
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Basic
body: It was the second such appointment in eight days. The Ocala paper is dated the third of December; Bainbridge named him Flight Sergeant on the eleventh. Counted from the day the first one took effect — November 3 — the same test ran twice, at two fields, inside five weeks: whether a cadet who could fly could also be trusted to answer for other cadets.

title: Basic
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Basic
body: The class book for Class 44-D survives in the collection. On the autograph page he listed himself as Squadron I, Flight “A,” and dated the entry December 16, 1943. The note beneath it is addressed to Joyce: “Darling; It seems like 10 years today I’ve been away from you instead of 10 months. Here’s hoping before long we’ll be able to see each other again. All My Love, Frankie.” (family collection).

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: Between Bainbridge and Hendricks sat one more rung this book had not previously accounted for. Frank's own qualification record lists advanced twin-engine training at Turner Field, Georgia, completed in April 1944 — two months after Bainbridge's single-engine basics, four months before Hendricks put him in a B-17. It was the intermediate step the pipeline required before trusting a cadet with four engines at once: a heavier, faster aircraft than anything in basic, and still nothing like the Fortress waiting at the end of it.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: Two documents now fix the stage's final week precisely, arriving at the same date from two different directions.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: The first is a certificate: on 15 April 1944, at Turner Field, Georgia, Second Lieutenant Frank J. Calicura passed the Instrument Flight Test prescribed by A.A.F. Regulation 50-3, signed by John B. Patrick, Colonel, Air Corps, commanding, and countersigned by the instrument check pilot, Major Wm. H. Jenkins, A.C. (family collection).

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: The second is the commission itself. A letter from Headquarters, Army Air Forces Eastern Flying Training Command, Maxwell Field, Alabama, addressed to Second Lieutenant Frank James Calicura at Turner Field, Albany, Georgia, informs him that the Secretary of War has directed that the President has appointed and commissioned him a temporary Second Lieutenant, Army of the United States, effective that same date — 15 April 1944 — under serial number A O-828662, the same number this book has already carried forward from the will signed at Avon Park five months later. The letter is issued by command of Major General Hanley and signed by the Adjutant General, Jamison Porter (family collection).

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: Read together, the two documents settle what earlier research had only inferred: commission and instrument qualification landed on the same day, certified from two different headquarters — Turner Field signing off the flying, Maxwell Field signing off the rank. Gold bars and instrument rating arrived in the same week’s mail, the way the advanced twin-engine pipeline was built to work.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: The Gazette put it in a paragraph headed Martinez Boy Now Lieut. in Air Corps. Aviation Cadet Frank James Calicura, son of Mr. and Mrs. Sam Calicura, Sr., 515 Mellius street — the paper’s spelling — commissioned a second lieutenant at Turner Field, Albany, Georgia, Colonel John B. Patrick announcing it that day. Patrick is the same name on the instrument certificate. The paper uses the parents’ house, and misspells the street. Frank had lived at 731 since 1938.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: A third document, dated to the same graduation week, rates him for the aeronautical designation itself rather than the commission or the instrument qualification. Personnel Orders Number 15, Headquarters Army Air Forces Eastern Flying Training Command, Maxwell Field, Alabama, 7 April 1944, lists the entire graduating roster of Class 44-D — dozens of names, alphabetically, Calicura's among them — as rated Pilot effective 15 April 1944, Turner Field, Albany, Georgia, under Army Air Forces Regulation 50-7 (family collection). Three separate documents converge on the same date: instrument qualification, officer’s commission, and pilot rating, each issued by a different office, each landing on 15 April 1944.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: A fourth item survives from the same week, and it belongs to a different category. Where the commission, the instrument certificate, and the pilot rating are administrative — records the Army kept because it had to — this one is a keepsake. A formal graduation announcement from the Army Air Forces Eastern Flying Training Command announces the graduation of Class 44-D, Turner Field, Albany, Georgia, on Saturday, April 15, 1944, personalized on its inside flap: Frank J. Calicura, Lieutenant, Air Forces, Army of the United States (family collection). Nothing about it was required. It was kept because a graduation is the kind of thing a family wants a card for, even one issued by the Army.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: One more object survives from Turner Field, and it is the only thing in this stretch of the record made to be worn. It is a ring: a dark stone in an oval bezel, the lettering around the bezel worn most of the way down to illegible, and on the shoulder an eagle with its wings spread over a shield. Beneath the shield is a banner with one word on it. PILOT.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: The paper from that April is all addressed to somebody — the Adjutant General, the Commanding General, whoever filed the qualification record. The ring is not addressed to anyone. It states what he was, in one word, to whoever happened to be looking at his hand.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: The night of the graduation itself is documented too, and not the way anyone at the ceremony would have chosen. A Gazette clipping headlined "Calicura Learns Hard Way How to Land in Tornado" reports that at midnight the Saturday of his commissioning, a tornado grounded every aircraft at Turner Field, a few hours before Frank was due to fly home on furlough — word reaching Joyce, at 731 Mellus Street, by telegram. He was expected within a few days if the furlough could still be arranged (family collection). The same clipping places the rest of the family on that same date: Dominic, commissioned a fighter pilot at Spence Field, Moultrie, Georgia; Nick, a Chief Petty Officer awaiting sailing orders at Alameda Naval Base; and Bill, stationed at Nashville, Tennessee, in the Army's antiaircraft artillery — the first documented record in this book of Bill's own wartime service, previously known only from his postwar partnership in the family's meat market.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: A second Gazette item from the same commissioning week names the transfer and the other three. Lt. Frank Calicura, Newly Commissioned, Soon to Get Transfer — Florida next. One of four brothers in the service. Corporal William Calicura in the anti-aircraft forces at Camp Davis, North Carolina; Nick a machinist’s mate in the Navy at Alameda; Dominic in the Army Air Corps at Moultrie, Georgia. The tornado clipping from the Saturday of that week puts Bill in Nashville and Nick a chief petty officer awaiting sailing orders. Two papers, two ranks, two stations. They are left standing.

title: Turner Field
titleText: Nine Hundred Miles South Turner Field
body: An earlier draft of this section stated that nothing in the family’s collection documented this stage beyond the bare entry on the qualification record. That statement no longer holds.

title: A School for One Thing
titleText: The Specialist A School for One Thing
body: Frank Calicura went to Hendricks Field to become a specific kind of pilot, and nothing else.

title: A School for One Thing
titleText: The Specialist A School for One Thing
body: The base had not always worked that way. It opened in January 1942 as a general combat crew school — pilots, copilots, navigators, bombardiers, engineers, radio operators, and gunners trained there together, as complete crews, through most of that first year. But in January 1943, more than a year before Frank arrived, the Army Air Forces reorganized Hendricks into something narrower: a specialized school for four-engine first pilots alone. From that point forward, the rest of a combat crew was assembled elsewhere. A man who came to Hendricks in the summer of 1944 came as a pilot candidate and nothing more — not yet responsible for nine other names, because he did not yet have nine other names to be responsible for.

title: A School for One Thing
titleText: The Specialist A School for One Thing
body: That distinction is easy to miss and matters. Frank did not meet the men he would eventually fly with at Hendricks. He met an airplane.

title: The Fortress
titleText: The Specialist The Fortress
body: What he met was larger than anything he had flown, heavier in every line, built to survive damage rather than to move quickly.

title: The Fortress
titleText: The Specialist The Fortress
body: The transition from twin-engine advanced training to a four-engine heavy bomber was the largest single jump in the entire pipeline. A B-17 had ten stations, four engines that had to be managed as a coordinated system rather than four separate problems, and no autopilot capable of holding formation on its own for the hours a mission actually required. Formation flying at altitude was manual labor as much as it was piloting — continuous small corrections, sustained for as long as the mission demanded, in an unpressurized aircraft at heights that were themselves a physical strain before anyone fired a shot.

title: The Fortress
titleText: The Specialist The Fortress
body: A cadet who had soloed a Stearman biplane a little over a year earlier was now expected to command a machine that weighed roughly thirty times as much and answered far less quickly to anything he did with his hands.

title: The Voucher
titleText: The Specialist The Voucher
body: Before Frank Calicura ever put a B-17 through its paces, the Army made sure he was dressed for it.

title: The Voucher
titleText: The Specialist The Voucher
body: Shipping Officer's Voucher No. 13, prepared in Frank's own hand and dated July 25, 1944, itemizes fifteen pieces of personal flying gear issued to him at Hendricks Field: a flyer's kit bag, summer and winter flying caps sized to his own head, a CO-2 cylinder, flying goggles, winter flying gloves, a winter and a summer flying helmet, a flying jacket, flying shoes, a summer flying suit, winter flying trousers, a flying vest, a life-preserver vest, and a mechanic's sweater. The whole issue was authorized under AAF Regulation 15-121, dated December 27, 1943, and countersigned by M. W. Hiller, Captain, Air Corps.

title: The Voucher
titleText: The Specialist The Voucher
body: Hiller's own title on the form reads AAF 95-Supply Officer, Hendricks Field. The number is a coincidence and nothing more — an internal Hendricks Field supply designation, seven months before Frank Calicura would ever hear of the 95th Bomb Group he was eventually assigned to. The two numbers have nothing to do with each other, and this book does not connect them.

title: The Voucher
titleText: The Specialist The Voucher
body: What the voucher actually documents is smaller and more concrete: a man being outfitted, piece by piece, sized and signed for, for a kind of flying he had not yet done.

title: Eight Dollars and Twelve Cents
titleText: The Specialist Eight Dollars and Twelve Cents
body: Not everything issued to him stayed issued. A Report of Survey filed at Hendricks Field on July 15, 1944 — ten days before the kit voucher above — records that an A-2 flying jacket belonging to Frank Calicura had been taken from a locker in Building 232, the Group I locker room, on or about July 8. The Army’s own accounting fixed its value at $8.12.

title: Eight Dollars and Twelve Cents
titleText: The Specialist Eight Dollars and Twelve Cents
body: The form required Frank to swear to the loss himself, which he did, in his own hand, before Norwyn W. Rees, a second lieutenant serving as recorder for the Property Adjustment Board: “I do solemnly swear... that the articles of public property shown above... were lost, destroyed, damaged, or worn out in the manner stated, while in the public service.” Sworn statement, notarized signature, official seal — all of it marshaled to formally account for one leather jacket, gone from a barracks locker at some point during a week in July 1944.

title: Eight Dollars and Twelve Cents
titleText: The Specialist Eight Dollars and Twelve Cents
body: It is a small theft, and the paperwork it generated outlasted it by decades. The Army’s bureaucracy, confronted with an eight-dollar loss, responded exactly as it would have to the loss of an engine: with a form, a witness, an oath, and a number carried to the cent. Whoever took the jacket left no other trace.

title: Ten Thousand Pilots
titleText: The Specialist Ten Thousand Pilots
body: Hendricks did this at a scale that is easy to state and hard to picture. At peak operation the field kept roughly 120 B-17s in service at once. Over the course of the war it trained more than ten thousand pilots to fly them — a number large enough that the base itself functioned as something closer to an industrial operation than a school, with a base population that at times ran several times the size of the town of Sebring around it.

title: Ten Thousand Pilots
titleText: The Specialist Ten Thousand Pilots
body: The field carried the name of a man the training itself had already killed. First Lieutenant Laird Woodruff Hendricks, a Florida native and 1939 West Point graduate, died in a B-17 crash in England on 28 July 1941 — three days after he had reported there to train other pilots, and five months before the United States had even entered the war. The base named for him spent the next three and a half years sending pilots toward the same continent that had killed him before a single American bomb had fallen on it.

title: Ten Thousand Pilots
titleText: The Specialist Ten Thousand Pilots
body: Hendricks’ own safety record was, by the standards of wartime flight training, a good one — and it still recorded nine fatal crashes and forty-five deaths before the war ended. Training a man to fly a four-engine bomber was dangerous in ways that had nothing to do with an enemy, and the base’s own numbers do not pretend otherwise.

title: Waiting for Nine Names
titleText: The Specialist Waiting for Nine Names
body: Frank Calicura left Hendricks Field in the summer of 1944 rated to fly the airplane. He still could not have named the man who would sit beside him in the right-hand seat, or the six who would work the positions behind him.

title: Waiting for Nine Names
titleText: The Specialist Waiting for Nine Names
body: That would happen next, at a different field, built for the purpose Hendricks had been narrowed to exclude: putting a trained pilot together with the rest of a crew for the first time. Frank knew, by the time he left Florida that summer, how to hold a B-17 level, how to manage four engines as a single problem instead of four, and how much weight he was now qualified to be responsible for in the air. He did not yet know who, specifically, he would be responsible for. That gap — a man who could fly the airplane, and a crew that did not exist yet — is where the next stage of his training began.

title: Waiting for Nine Names
titleText: The Specialist Waiting for Nine Names
body: A birth came first. Before the announcement card, a color plate of Joyce: 1943, the front of 731 Mellus Street, already carrying the son the Gazette would name. Another plate, standing, the same suit, another woman the family file names Marie.

title: Waiting for Nine Names
titleText: The Specialist Waiting for Nine Names
body: Frank James Calicura Jr. was born June 20, 1944, at 3:15 p.m., at Community Hospital in Martinez — seven pounds seven ounces, named for the father who had not yet seen him. The Gazette ran the news the next day under the headline "New ‘General’ at Lieut. Calicura Home," reporting that Frank, still training in Florida, had a new member of his family he had never seen, and that Joyce was reported "doing nicely" by hospital authorities. A handmade announcement card survives alongside the clipping, addressed in the family's own hand along a drawn clothesline: born 6/20/44, 3:15 P.M., named Frank James Calicura Jr., weighed 7 lbs. 7 oz., signed "Proud Mama and Papa, Joyce & Frank Calicura" (family collection). The envelope carrying the news to Frank is postmarked Martinez, June 21, 1944, addressed to Officer Student's Section, Class 44-D, Hendricks Field, Sebring, Florida (family collection) — reaching him roughly a month before his mother's death, and identifying the infant son shown with him in the undated family photograph cited below as this same child.

title: Waiting for Nine Names
titleText: The Specialist Waiting for Nine Names
body: Something else happened in that gap, and the collection records it in a newspaper rather than in any document the Army produced. On the night of Friday, July 21, 1944, after an illness of two days, Angelina Calicura died at Community Hospital in Martinez. She was fifty-eight. She had lived in the town thirty-seven years, kept the house at 515 Mellus Street, and was a native of Italy. The Martinez News-Gazette carried the notice the following morning under the heading Pioneer Mother Dies, and listed what she left behind: her husband Saverio, five sons, eight daughters, seven grandchildren, and two brothers — A. Rodia of Martinez and Sam Rodia of Los Angeles.

title: Waiting for Nine Names
titleText: The Specialist Waiting for Nine Names
body: Four of the sons were in uniform, and the paper gave their stations: Nick in the Navy, Dominic in Georgia, Corporal William, and Lieutenant Frank Calicura, in North Carolina — a detail that matches nothing else documented about Frank’s service that summer and is noted here without explanation. What can be said with confidence is where he actually was: home in Martinez, on a temporary leave from Hendricks Field, when his mother died. A photograph in the family’s collection shows him on the porch steps in uniform, holding the son he had not yet seen. The family dates it to this leave — the first time he met Jimmy, home for the funeral. His qualification record shows him in continuous B-17 transition training at Hendricks from April 16 to August 17, 1944, but that record does not conflict with the leave — it tracks a man’s official duty station, not his personal time away from it. A soldier on leave remains carried on his unit’s rolls; nothing about two weeks home in California would appear on the paperwork the qualification record was drawn from. Frank was there when the news came. He then went back. The funeral, the notice said, awaited word of the possible arrival of her sons from the south. Whether any of them reached it the collection does not record.

title: Waiting for Nine Names
titleText: The Specialist Waiting for Nine Names
body: Six weeks later, at Avon Park, Frank Calicura signed a will. It is dated September 7, 1944. He was a second lieutenant, serial number O-828662. He named Joyce B. Calicura of 731 Mellus Street, Martinez, as executrix and left her the entire estate, with his brother Sam of 3120 Ricks Court named to take it if she did not survive him. It is a form filled out by a twenty-three-year-old who had not yet flown a combat mission.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: Before Frank Calicura ever met the men he would fly with, the Army had already begun putting their names on paper — twice, three months apart, at two different fields.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: A Special Order issued August 30, 1944, from Headquarters, Third Air Force Replacement Depot, Tampa, Florida, formally constituted the crew — numbered 1479 in the surviving copy, though the number is partly obscured by a typewritten correction in the original — with Frank Calicura as pilot, Victor Probst as copilot, and six enlisted men beneath them: Earle Bogacki, Robert Brown, Marvin Markus, Robert Collins, Dale Ernest, and James Titus. No navigator appears on this order.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: A certificate from the same headquarters fixes the dates of that stretch precisely. Headquarters Third Air Force Replacement Depot, Plant Park, Tampa, Florida, certified on September 2, 1944, that Second Lieutenant Frank J. Calicura had not been assigned or occupied public quarters at his permanent station — Plant Park itself — from August 17 to September 2, 1944, both dates inclusive, because the quarters available there were inadequate for an officer with dependents, signed William H. Askey, Captain, AC, Adjutant (family collection). The dates close a gap this book had left open without noticing it: Frank's qualification record puts the end of his Hendricks Field training at August 17, 1944, and this certificate places him at Tampa starting that same day, continuously, until the Avon Park training record picks him up on September 2. There is no gap between Hendricks and Avon Park. There is Tampa, in between, for exactly sixteen days — and Joyce, already carried as his dependent, kept off the base the entire time by quarters the Army itself judged inadequate.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: The navigator's absence from the Tampa order closes in the next document. Special Orders No. 341, Headquarters Avon Park Army Air Field, dated November 6, 1944, lists the same eight men, now designated 3AF-NV-23 Crew No. 8, with a ninth name added: John R. Barnes, second lieutenant, navigator. The same order transferred the crew to Hunter Field, Georgia, to arrive November 20, 1944, and report to the Combat Crew Center of the Third Air Force Staging Wing — the same Hunter Field that appears again a month later in the shipping ticket already documented in this book, where all nine men signed for their flying gear before the last leg overseas.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: A third document fills the gap between that transfer order and the gear issue at Hunter Field. Special Orders Number 337, Headquarters Third Air Force Staging Wing, Hunter Field, Georgia, 2 December 1944, dispatches the crew overseas by air under Shipment FQ-555-CA, listing them as Crew FQ-555-CA-93, Project 92923R: Frank J. Calicura, pilot; Victor G. Probst, copilot; John R. Barnes, navigator; Earle F. Bogacki, engineer; Robert J. Brown, radio operator; Marvin L. Markus, Robert E. Collins, Dale S. Ernest, and James A. Titus, gunners — all nine names and serial numbers matching the crew already established here (family collection). The order routes them from Hunter Field to Dow Field, Bangor, Maine, via Grenier Field, New Hampshire, reporting to the Commanding General, Air Transport Command, for further dispatch to an overseas destination.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: The order also assigns them an aircraft for the movement: Ap. No. 44-6830, a B-17G — not 44-6838, the Spirit of Martinez. The two serials sit eight apart, and the reason is that they were built eight apart: both came out of Douglas production block B-17G-65-DL, serials 44-6751 through 44-6875. They were never the same airplane.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: 44-6830’s own record follows the order exactly. She was delivered to Hunter Field on November 23, 1944, and reached Grenier Field, New Hampshire, on December 13 — Hunter to Grenier, the route Special Orders Number 337 lays out, in the fortnight after the order was cut. She was the ferry ship. On the far side of the Atlantic the crew gave her up, as ferry crews generally did, and she went to a different group altogether: the 407th Bomb Squadron of the 92nd Bomb Group, at Podington, on March 4, 1945.

title: Crew No. 1479
titleText: Nine Strangers Crew No. 1479
body: She lasted fourteen days there. Battle damaged over Berlin on March 18, 1945, she force-landed in Poland and was written off on the twenty-sixth. By then Frank Calicura’s crew was most of the way through a tour in an aircraft built in the same shed, in the same block, the same month.

title: The Replacement Training Unit
titleText: Nine Strangers The Replacement Training Unit
body: Frank Calicura met the men he would fly with in Florida, in September 1944, at a base built to manufacture that meeting.

title: The Replacement Training Unit
titleText: Nine Strangers The Replacement Training Unit
body: Avon Park had not started out for this purpose. It opened in 1942 as a bombing and gunnery range, then trained medium-bomber crews for the 336th and 397th Bombardment Groups. In November 1943 the 88th Bombardment Group arrived from Walla Walla, Washington, to run B-17 operational training instead, and on 1 May 1944 the field was reorganized again and renamed for what it had by then become: the Avon Park Replacement Training Unit, Heavy Bombardment. Its whole function was to take pilots who had finished four-engine transition somewhere else — Hendricks Field, in Frank’s case — and put them together with the eight other men the Army had decided, on paper, belonged in the same airplane.

title: The Replacement Training Unit
titleText: Nine Strangers The Replacement Training Unit
body: No one at Avon Park asked whether the nine of them would get along. The unit’s job was to teach them to work, not to like each other, though most crews managed both before it was over.

title: The Range
titleText: Nine Strangers The Range
body: What Avon Park actually taught a crew was not flying. Every man aboard already knew how to do his own job, or was expected to by the time he arrived. What the base taught was working together against something that would shoot back.

title: The Range
titleText: Nine Strangers The Range
body: The range itself was built to simulate it. Engineers had laid out a mock town of some five hundred fifty-five acres on the shore of Lake Arbuckle, purpose-built for a crew to practice finding and hitting a target that looked like the ones waiting in Germany. A floating target sat out on Lake Kissimmee for the bombardier and the pilot to coordinate a run against water instead of ground. An eight-mile stretch of dummy railroad gave them something long and thin to walk their bombs down, the way railyards actually behaved as targets. Later in the war, instructors from the Army Air Forces School of Applied Tactics in Orlando built a specialized incendiary target as well, as the target list overseas shifted toward that kind of raid.

title: The Range
titleText: Nine Strangers The Range
body: None of it was Germany. All of it was built to feel, procedurally, like Germany would.
