title: Nine Names
titleText: Nine Strangers Nine Names
body: The crew that trained together at Avon Park, and would fly together over Europe six months later, had nine names on it.

title: Nine Names
titleText: Nine Strangers Nine Names
body: Frank Calicura, pilot. Victor G. Probst, copilot. John R. Barnes, navigator. Marvin L. Markus, togglier. Earle F. Bogacki, flight engineer and top turret gunner. Robert J. Brown, radio operator. Robert E. Collins, Dale S. Ernest, and James A. Titus, gunners.

title: Nine Names
titleText: Nine Strangers Nine Names
body: Barnes was born in Philadelphia on January 31, 1922, the son of Leonard and Gertrude Barnes of Emporium, Pennsylvania. Probst would later study architecture; at the time he was simply the copilot. Markus came from Kingfisher, Oklahoma — the town already named on the wallet that would later be stamped for the crew. Bogacki had been born in Cleveland in 1920 to Frank and Stella Bojack, a surname the family later changed to Bogacki (which is very likely why a contemporary wallet clipping misprinted a Cleveland man’s name as “Nogacki” and still got the city right). Brown was born May 1, 1924, in Corning, New York, to a Polish immigrant father. Ernest came from West Virginia. Titus’s own record comes into focus through two wartime clippings from what internal evidence points to as a Lincoln, Nebraska paper. The first places him, as a corporal, having landed in England after graduating gunnery school at Las Vegas in June 1944. The second records his later discharge as a sergeant from L.A.A.F. — almost certainly Lincoln Army Air Field — and names his parents as Mr. and Mrs. Joe B. Titus of 3343 LaSalle Street. Both state plainly that he served in England as tail gunner on a B-17: a fourth independent source for a fact the record had already secured three times over.

title: Nine Names
titleText: Nine Strangers Nine Names
body: Robert E. Collins’s identity is anchored across two independent wartime records. His WWII draft registration gives the Hutchinson, Kansas residence and employment at the Coca-Cola Bottling Company; a shipping ticket from December 1944 carries an actual wartime signature reading “Robert E. Collins,” consistent with the one on the draft card. He was not yet twenty when he registered, working under a boss named Lewis Scruggs, with a next-of-contact listed as Margaret Dappen at 221 East First Street. Born October 5, 1923, he had grown up and gone to work in one small Kansas city before the ball turret of a B-17 became his job instead.

title: Nine Names
titleText: Nine Strangers Nine Names
body: That shipping ticket turns out to carry more than Collins’s signature. The full document — a complete copy of a page previously seen only in part — shows the entire crew signing together on December 13, 1944, the ticket issued out of Hunter Field, Georgia and drawn at the 177th AAF Base Unit, Grenier Field, Manchester, New Hampshire, for flying jackets and trousers before the last leg overseas: Calicura as pilot, Probst as copilot, Barnes as navigator, Bogacki as engineer, and Brown, Markus, Collins, Ernest, and Titus in their turret and gunner positions, nine signatures in two columns on a single government form. A tenth name appears beside them — Eugene P. Allamano, listed as “RAD” — who was not part of the combat crew at all, but a passenger carried on that same overseas ferry flight in late December 1944, gone from the record as quickly as he appears in it.

title: Nine Names
titleText: Nine Strangers Nine Names
body: In September 1944, none of that had happened yet. They were nine men who had been assigned to the same airplane and told to learn to trust it, and each other, before anyone put a target under them.

title: The Bill
titleText: Nine Strangers The Bill
body: Somewhere in this stretch of training — the collection does not fix an exact date — a dollar bill went around a room and came back covered in signatures.

title: The Bill
titleText: Nine Strangers The Bill
body: Frank signed it. Dominic signed it. Other names on it belong to local airmen the family can no longer fully place, and possibly to a tradition Sam Calicura Jr. had a hand in starting, back at the field on the Martinez waterfront where all of this had, in one sense, begun. A short snorter carried no military significance whatsoever. The Army did not require it, did not track it, and would not have cared if it were lost. It survived only because someone decided it was worth keeping, which is a different kind of significance than the Army’s.

title: The Bill
titleText: Nine Strangers The Bill
body: It is the only surviving record of a night none of the nine of them wrote an account of. No letter describes it. No clipping mentions it. What happened in that room exists now only as a list of names on a piece of currency. That is how most of what happens between men in wartime survives: not in the official record, but on whatever scrap was in a pocket when it seemed worth writing something down.

title: New York, December 1944
titleText: Nine Strangers New York, December 1944
body: Between Avon Park and the ocean, Frank Calicura and his brother Dominic saw each other one more time.

title: New York, December 1944
titleText: Nine Strangers New York, December 1944
body: A Gazette clipping, undated in the collection but internally dated by its own content, places Frank on the East Coast in December 1944, “awaiting assignment to duty, presumably in the European Theatre of action” — his crew having, in the paper’s words, “recently completed all training assignments at a southern flying field,” a description that matches Avon Park exactly. The same clipping states that Dominic, “pilot of a fighter plane and now instructing at a Georgia field,” had “recently got together with Frank in New York during a brief leave.” A photograph in the family’s collection, captioned in period handwriting “Frank & Dominick Calicura,” shows the two of them at a table in uniform, pilot wings visible on both men — very likely the same meeting the clipping describes, though nothing in either source fixes the two together beyond the coincidence of timing.

title: New York, December 1944
titleText: Nine Strangers New York, December 1944
body: One detail in the clipping does not match anything else in this book. It gives Frank’s crew as eleven men. Every other source — the nine names established in §6.4, the shipping ticket bearing nine crew signatures and one additional passenger — accounts for at most ten people ever associated with the aircraft, combat crew and passenger together. “Eleven” is not derived from anything else in the record, and it is treated here the same way this book has treated every other hometown-paper figure that doesn’t square with the operational documents: stated, not corrected.

title: The Ground
titleText: Station 119 The Ground
body: Horham was planned for the Royal Air Force, then handed to the United States Army Air Forces in 1942 and given the designation Station 119. It sat four miles southeast of Eye, in East Suffolk, and it was large enough that it did not belong to a single village — the base sprawled across four parishes, Horham, Denham, Redlingfield, and Hoxne, none of which had been consulted in any meaningful way about acquiring it.

title: The Ground
titleText: Station 119 The Ground
body: It was built to the standard Class A layout: three intersecting runways, the main one running about two thousand metres, the two secondary runways about fourteen hundred each. Two T-2 hangars went up on the south side, painted in black and dark earth camouflage — an earlier practice than the tar varnish finish used at fields built later in the war. The technical site sat beside them along the B1117 road to Eye. Headquarters, the administrative buildings, and the living sites were temporary Nissen hut construction, dispersed westward into the farmland of Denham parish so that a single raid could not take out the whole station at once.

title: The Ground
titleText: Station 119 The Ground
body: A landscape historian has described the construction of the airfield as the single largest change to that landscape in two thousand years. It is not an exaggerated claim. By 1943 there were more than a hundred thousand American airmen in England, most of them in East Anglia, and more than a hundred RAF and USAAF bases packed into an area smaller than Connecticut. Horham alone held roughly seventy aircraft and thirty-five hundred personnel — more people on the base than in the villages around it.

title: The Ground
titleText: Station 119 The Ground
body: The men lived in metal huts through English winters with pot-bellied stoves for heat. Frank's own Certificate of Service puts his arrival in the European theater on January 6, 1945 — a date this book previously gave, without a document behind it, as the first of the month. It is corrected here.

title: The Reputation
titleText: Station 119 The Reputation
body: He was joining a unit whose defining history was already finished.

title: The Reputation
titleText: Station 119 The Reputation
body: The 95th Bombardment Group had come to Horham on 15 June 1943 after short stays at Alconbury and Framlingham, and stayed for the rest of the war. It flew four squadrons of B-17s — the 334th, 335th, 336th, and 412th — and from September 1943 the base also served as headquarters for the 13th Combat Bombardment Wing of the 3rd Air Division, which meant Horham directed not only its own group but the 100th at Thorpe Abbotts and the 390th at Framlingham.

title: The Reputation
titleText: Station 119 The Reputation
body: What set the 95th apart was three Distinguished Unit Citations, more than any other bomb group in the Eighth Air Force. The first came for Regensburg on 17 August 1943. The second for Münster on 10 October 1943. The third for Berlin on 4 March 1944, when the 95th became the first American group to bomb the German capital — flying through weather that turned back or diverted most of the other groups sent that day, and hitting the target anyway.

title: The Reputation
titleText: Station 119 The Reputation
body: All three of those days were behind it before Frank Calicura ever saw the place. The men who earned them were, by January 1945, dead, imprisoned, rotated home, or reassigned elsewhere. A replacement crew arriving at Horham inherited a reputation entire and instantly, having contributed nothing to it, and was expected to fly as though it had.

title: The Reputation
titleText: Station 119 The Reputation
body: Martinez learned the same inheritance in a paragraph headed Lieut. Calicura At British Base. Second Lieutenant Frank J. Calicura, 23, assigned to the 95th Bombardment Group, commanded by Colonel Jack E. Shuck of Casper, Wyo., taking an orientation course on flying procedure prior to combat. The paper then recites the group’s citations: the first American bombing attack on Berlin; Münster, October 1943; the England-Africa shuttle to a Messerschmitt plant at Regensburg, August 1943. It is the hometown version of the reputation this chapter has already named. The paper puts his father at 731 Mellus Street, with Joyce and Frank Jr. living with him. This book puts the parents at 515 and Frank at 731. After Angelina’s death the household may have moved; the paper may have mixed the two doors. Age twenty-three fits.

title: The Colonel
titleText: Station 119 The Colonel
body: Command of the group changed hands five times in under two years.

title: The Colonel
titleText: Station 119 The Colonel
body: Colonel Jack E. Shuck took it over in December 1944 — the same month Frank’s crew received the operations order that would send them to England. Shuck was therefore the group’s commanding officer for essentially the whole of Frank Calicura’s combat tour, from the first mission in February through the end of the group’s operational life in April.

title: The Colonel
titleText: Station 119 The Colonel
body: A photograph in the family’s collection shows the two men shaking hands. It is dated 1945 and it is what it appears to be: a formal recognition moment, the kind a group commander performed regularly and a crew photographed once. The book records it as that and does not inflate it into a friendship the record gives no evidence for.

title: The Colonel
titleText: Station 119 The Colonel
body: There would be one more commander. Lieutenant Colonel Robert H. Stuart took over the 95th on 28 April 1945 — eight days before the war in Europe ended, and four days before the group began dropping food instead of bombs. It is Stuart’s name on the memorandum in the family’s collection recommending Frank as an instructor and certifying, in the flat language of a headquarters document, exactly how many times he had gone out and how many hours he had spent doing it, written in the last weeks the 95th Bomb Group existed as a fighting unit.

title: The Red Feather
titleText: Station 119 The Red Feather
body: The group’s emblem was a red feather on a shield.

title: The Red Feather
titleText: Station 119 The Red Feather
body: In March 1944 the non-commissioned officers of the ground crews, who had no club of their own, opened one in a set of interconnected Nissen huts on one of the communal sites and named it after the emblem: the Red Feather Club. It had a beer hall, a bar, and a dry lounge. In 1944 a staff sergeant named Nathan Bindler painted murals on the walls of one of the rooms. They are still there.

title: The Red Feather
titleText: Station 119 The Red Feather
body: This is the part of a bomber station that the operational record does not touch at all. The mission reports document targets, tonnage, losses, and times. They document nothing about a beer hall, a mural, a cartoon pinned to a barracks wall, or a card from a Soho club carried back from a London pass and kept in a uniform pocket for the rest of a man’s life. The family’s collection preserves a “Barracks E” cartoon and a Red Bar membership card from Green’s Court, Soho — two scraps of a daily life that ran continuously alongside the missions and was almost entirely undocumented by anyone whose job it was to document things. The coat still had the rest of that pocket in it: three paper prophylactics, laid on the flap as they came out, with the same card underneath.

title: The Red Feather
titleText: Station 119 The Red Feather
body: The collection also holds photographs of other crews from the 95th — Lieutenant Dillon’s, Shaw’s, Olson’s. They survive for no better reason than proximity: those men were quartered near enough to Frank’s crew, or flew near enough to them, that the prints ended up in the same collection. That is how the social world of a bomb group is reconstructed now, when it is reconstructed at all — from who happened to be standing next to whom. The prints date themselves. Shaw’s is 27 February 1944, a year before this crew reached Horham. Dillon’s is 26 December 1944, eleven days before Frank’s Certificate of Service places him in England. The family identifies both as 335th. Olson’s has not been found in this pass.

title: The Red Feather
titleText: Station 119 The Red Feather
body: By the middle of January 1945, Frank Calicura’s crew was settled on a station whose great days were behind it, under a commander who had arrived the same month they did, in a metal hut in a Suffolk field, waiting for their names to appear on a board.

title: The Order
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Order
body: On the morning of February 3, 1945, one of the largest American bombing missions of the war took off from airfields across East Anglia, bound for Berlin.

title: The Order
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Order
body: Just over a thousand B-17s were dispatched, escorted by long-range fighters that finally, by this stage of the war, could accompany them the entire distance. The order named the Friedrichstrasse railway station as the aiming point — a target in the heart of the city, chosen deliberately for its location. General Jimmy Doolittle, commanding the Eighth Air Force, objected when he received it. To him, an aiming point that close to the city center amounted to bombing Berlin itself rather than a military objective. He raised the objection to his superior, General Carl Spaatz, and was overruled. The mission flew as ordered.

title: The Order
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Order
body: The bomber stream stretched some 360 miles and took roughly ninety minutes to pass over the city. Berlin’s defenses — forty miles of searchlights, flak batteries, and decoy fires, still backed by enough fighter aircraft to make the approach dangerous even this late in the war — met the formation in full. A lieutenant colonel leading the 91st Bomb Group over the target that day did not come home. Neither did eight aircraft of the 95th Bomb Group.

title: The Order
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Order
body: Frank Calicura’s group. Frank Calicura’s base.

title: The Eleventh Day
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Eleventh Day
body: He had been at Horham a little under a month.

title: The Eleventh Day
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Eleventh Day
body: Frank's Certificate of Service places his arrival in England on January 6, 1945, not the first of the month this book had previously assumed without a document behind it. His qualification record gives a formal assignment date to the 335th Bomb Squadron, 95th Bomb Group, of January 11, 1945 — five days into the process described here, not the ten this book had calculated from the earlier, unsourced date — orientation, local flying, the accumulation of currency in the aircraft and the theater before a new crew was trusted with a combat assignment. He was not on the February 3 mission, and no record suggests his crew was ever slated for it. New crews simply were not yet in rotation for a raid of that scale and risk, and the absence of his name from that day’s loss list is not a near miss to be dramatized — it is the ordinary consequence of being new.

title: The Eleventh Day
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Eleventh Day
body: Frank's own Individual Flight Record survives for this exact window, and it turns "orientation, local flying, the accumulation of currency" into specific numbers. A supplemental entry for December 1944 logs a single B-17G flight, 5 hours 10 minutes as first pilot, with an hour of instrument time. January 1945 adds three more B-17G flights before combat began — 8 hours 30 minutes, 5 hours 25 minutes, and 1 hour 30 minutes as first pilot, 15 hours 25 minutes in all — alongside three one-hour sessions in the Link trainer, the ground-based instrument simulator every crew used to keep instrument skills current between actual flights. The record is certified by Robert J. Lynch, Captain, Air Corps, Assistant Operations Officer, 95th Bomb Group (family collection).

title: The Eleventh Day
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Eleventh Day
body: The same document gives a transfer date to the 335th Bomb Squadron of January 14, 1945 — three days later than the January 11 date already established here from the qualification record. The two documents do not explain the difference.

title: The Eleventh Day
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Eleventh Day
body: But he was there. Whatever the station felt like on the evening of February 3, with eight crews’ worth of empty bunks and gear still hanging where men had left it that morning, Frank Calicura felt it too, from inside the same huts, eleven days before he would fly his own first mission from the same airfield.

title: The Eleventh Day
titleText: Eight Empty Places The Eleventh Day
body: No letter, no clipping, and no document in the family’s collection records what that evening was like, or what Frank made of it. The silence itself is worth stating plainly rather than filled in.

title: What the Board Would Ask
titleText: Eight Empty Places What the Board Would Ask
body: Missions like February 3 were not routine, but the machinery that produced them was.

title: What the Board Would Ask
titleText: Eight Empty Places What the Board Would Ask
body: Every operational day at Horham began with the same sequence: a board posted before dawn naming which squadrons and crews would fly, briefings that revealed the target only once the crews were assembled, the long wait through assembly and the Channel crossing, and eventually a debriefing hut that either filled with the right number of men or did not. For eleven days after February 3, Frank Calicura was not yet part of that sequence. He was watching it happen to other crews, from the outside, in a station that had just taken its heaviest loss in recent memory and would go on flying missions the next day, and the day after that, because that was what the schedule required regardless of what the debriefing hut had looked like the night before.

title: What the Board Would Ask
titleText: Eight Empty Places What the Board Would Ask
body: On the morning of February 14, a name went up on the board that had not been there before. It was his.

title: The Board
titleText: Mission One The Board
body: The name Frank Calicura had been waiting to see went up before dawn on February 14.

title: The Board
titleText: Mission One The Board
body: A mission day at Horham followed the same sequence regardless of the target: wake in the dark, a hurried breakfast, briefing in a room that filled with cigarette smoke before the curtain came off the map. Only then did a crew learn where they were going. For Frank Calicura’s crew, on this particular morning, the answer was Chemnitz — a marshalling yard in Saxony, part of the rail network still moving German men and material toward a collapsing eastern front.

title: The Board
titleText: Mission One The Board
body: It was, by the standards of the war by that point, an enormous operation. The Eighth Air Force dispatched 1,377 bombers and 962 fighters that day, aimed at oil and rail targets across Germany — one of the largest single-day efforts the Eighth would mount. The force split roughly in two. Four hundred sixty-one B-17s were sent to hit the marshalling yard at Dresden. A separate force of four hundred fifty-seven B-17s — Frank’s among them — was sent to hit the marshalling yard at Chemnitz, roughly forty miles away. Of that second force, 294 aircraft found and bombed the primary target; the rest, turned back by weather or unable to identify it, dropped instead on airfields and rail yards at Eger, Bamberg, Sonneberg, Tachau, and Hof. Losses on the Chemnitz mission were, in the arithmetic of that war, light: one B-17 lost, a handful of casualties. Frank’s crew came home.

title: The Board
titleText: Mission One The Board
body: A map in the scrapbook circles Chemnitz among that week’s raids. A number in the margin may be 7 or 8. This book numbers Chemnitz first. The circle and the number are both in the collection.

title: The Same Morning
titleText: Mission One The Same Morning
body: Chemnitz was not Dresden. The distinction matters, and the record keeps it.

title: The Same Morning
titleText: Mission One The Same Morning
body: But the two missions launched within the same operation, on the same morning, from bases scattered across the same corner of England, and any account of February 14, 1945 has to hold both facts without letting one blur into the other. The night before, RAF Bomber Command had struck Dresden with roughly eight hundred aircraft, followed at midday by the separate American force of 461 B-17s that bombed through smoke still rising fifteen thousand feet from the fires of the night before. That was not Frank Calicura’s mission. His squadron never approached Dresden’s airspace that day. What can be said is only this: on the single morning of his first combat mission, in the same hour, from airfields not far from his own, roughly seven hundred American aircrew were flying toward a city that would become one of the most argued-over targets of the entire war, while Frank Calicura and four hundred fifty-six other B-17s were flying toward a rail yard forty miles away that, by comparison, history has mostly forgotten.

title: The Same Morning
titleText: Mission One The Same Morning
body: Neither the collection nor the manuscript records what, if anything, Frank knew or thought about Dresden that day. The clipping the family kept — “Key Rail City Near Capital Is Pounded” — describes his own mission, not the other one. The timing is a coincidence, and nothing more should be put in his mouth about a raid he did not fly.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: What Chemnitz meant to Frank Calicura personally was smaller and more exact than what it meant to the war. It was the first entry.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: His own accounting, recorded later in his own hand, would eventually run to twenty-eight combat missions and three humanitarian ones — thirty-one in total, against an original tour requirement of thirty-five. Chemnitz was where that count began. Every subsequent number attached to Frank Calicura’s war — the twenty-six on the Lucky Bastard Club card, the thirty bomb symbols painted on his jacket, the twenty-eight his commanding officer would certify, the thirty-one that only appears when two documents are read together, the forty-eight a hometown newspaper would eventually print, the fifty-three missions the aircraft itself would fly before the war ended — all of it starts counting from this one morning, this one rail yard, this one mission that was not the famous one happening forty miles away at the same hour.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: He flew home, was debriefed in a hut that smelled of cigarettes and wet sheepskin and coffee that had been on the stove since before the first ship came back, and went to sleep with twenty-seven missions still ahead of him, not knowing yet that the number would change twice more before the war let him stop counting.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: The 95th Bomb Group’s own crew record settles a detail the family’s clipping had left ambiguous. The headline read “Chemnitz/Cottbus,” as though the two were one target. They were not. Chemnitz was mission one, on the fourteenth. Cottbus was mission two, flown the very next day, February 15. Frank Calicura’s war did not begin with a single mission. It began with two, back to back, before he had been in combat forty-eight hours.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: The second of them cost the group two aircraft. One was Big Casino, C. D. Schaad’s B-17 of the 335th Squadron — Frank’s own squadron, on Frank’s second day of the war. Her Missing Air Crew Report, number 12378, is a record of an aircraft simply falling out of the sky over a period of half an hour: at 1142, with her number two engine feathered, she lagged behind the formation; at 1212 she was last seen heading northwest; she crashed at Tillowitz. The report gives two map coordinates, two timestamps, and a direction. It does not say what happened in between, because nobody watching was in a position to see. The other was Easy Going, F. W. Volz of the 336th. A different squadron. The compilation records both.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: The same crew record settles something else about that first morning, and it runs against the way this book has described the crew up to now. On February 14, 1945, Frank Calicura flew the Spirit of Martinez with Barnes navigating, Markus in the nose, Brown on the radio, Bogacki in the top turret, Collins in the ball, Ernest at a waist gun and Titus in the tail — seven of the eight men he had trained with at Avon Park. The eighth was not aboard. In the right-hand seat that day was Richard J. Austin, a name that appears nowhere else in the family’s collection.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: Victor Probst flew that morning too, in a different airplane. The crew record puts him in the right-hand seat of The Red Fox, co-piloting for John V. Bradley, with eight men whose names do not otherwise touch this account. The two aircraft went to the same target, in the same formation, and came back to the same field.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: Nothing in the family’s collection explains the arrangement, but the crew record itself does. Richard J. Austin was not a name pulled from a pool. He was John Bradley’s own co-pilot, and appears in the right-hand seat of Bradley’s crew on its other missions that spring. Bradley’s crew had been flying combat since January, through Mannheim and Neuss and Duisburg and Weimar, well before Frank Calicura reached Horham.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: What happened on February 14 was therefore not an assignment but a trade, between two particular crews. Bradley gave up his co-pilot to the new crew for the day and took the new crew’s co-pilot with him. Frank Calicura flew his first mission with a man who had already done a dozen; Victor Probst flew his sitting beside a pilot who had. It was the Eighth Air Force’s standard way of putting a new crew over Germany the first time, and here the crew record shows the two halves of it in the same formation, on the same morning, going to the same rail yard. One mission.

title: Twenty-Eight to Go
titleText: Mission One Twenty-Eight to Go
body: What the record does show is that the crew this book has called nine strangers, and then simply the crew, did not all fly their first mission together — and that when they did assemble in the Spirit of Martinez, it was already, for seven of them, the second day of the war. Neither man appears in the other’s aircraft again.

title: Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
body: The 95th Bomb Group’s own crew record shows what produced it. After Chemnitz and Cottbus on the fourteenth and fifteenth, the run continued.

title: Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
body: Frank Calicura’s crew flew again on the nineteenth to Osnabrück, then the twentieth to Nuremberg, then the twenty-first to Nuremberg again, the twenty-second, Bamberg, the twenty-fourth, Bremen, the twenty-fifth, Munich, the twenty-seventh, Leipzig.

title: Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
body: One of these has a clipping of its own beyond those already quoted.

title: Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
body: Osnabrück, the third mission, “1,100 Heavies Hit Nazi Rails,” reporting objectives at Osnabrück, Rheine, and Seiger and areas across the Ruhr, escorted by some five hundred Mustangs and Thunderbolts that strafed communication lines below.

title: Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
body: Nine missions in fourteen days, several of them on consecutive or near-consecutive mornings, each one requiring the same sequence — wake before dawn, briefing, the long climb to altitude, hours in an unpressurized aircraft at temperatures that could freeze exposed skin in minutes, the bomb run, the equally long flight home, debrief.

title: Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Nine Missions in Fourteen Days
body: No mission in that run stands alone in the way Chemnitz does, as a first. They accumulate instead, one against the next, in a tempo the flight record reduces to a single figure. The men who flew it would have measured it in a different currency: how many hours of sleep separated one wake-up call from the last.

title: Munich, February 25
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Munich, February 25
body: Mission eight took Frank Calicura’s crew to Munich — a rail target, not an airfield, though two clippings in the collection share that city and a nearly identical headline, and only the 95th Bomb Group’s dated crew record sorts out which belongs to which mission.

title: Munich, February 25
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Munich, February 25
body: The family’s own clipping survives from this one: “Rail-Hitting Heavies Tear Into Munich,” reporting that Fortresses rumbled over the city in two waves to hit the terminal rail station and marshalling yards in its eastern and western districts, the fourth day in a row the Eighth had thrown its weight against German communications and fuel supplies. Other formations that same day struck the yards at Ulm, a tank assembly plant at Aschaffenburg, airfields at Giebelstadt and Schwebisch-Hall, and an oil depot hidden in the woods outside Neuberg. More than seven hundred Mustangs and Thunderbolts escorted the raid, five hundred of them assigned solely to shield the bombers. The clipping is a fair measure of how large and how routine this kind of effort had become by February 1945 — a rail network under sustained, systematic attack, one city at a time, as a matter of course rather than exception.

title: Munich, February 25
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Munich, February 25
body: The ninth morning was Leipzig, February 27. The Air Medal is dated that day. The family kept no clipping of this one of its own.

title: Three Missions Without a Story
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Three Missions Without a Story
body: Between Leipzig and Swinemünde, the crew record shows three more missions the family kept clippings for but never a story about. Each of them carries a number in the scrapbook and nothing else — no mark, no note, nothing to distinguish it from the rest of a working week.

title: Three Missions Without a Story
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Three Missions Without a Story
body: March 3 took them to Brunswick, an aircraft-manufacturing center the Eighth Air Force returned to repeatedly that spring — not a single decisive strike but one of several passes at the same industry, the kind of target that required hitting more than once to matter.

title: Three Missions Without a Story
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Three Missions Without a Story
body: That same mission cost the group something the log entry does not gesture toward. The 95th put up thirty-seven aircraft that morning. The group’s own tally for the day records one damaged and one lost. The one lost was not lost over the target. The Missing Air Crew Report, number 12889, sets out the sequence in the flat register such reports use. At 1024, Stacy J. Tavis’s aircraft — Aunt Callie’s Baby — lost its position and fell behind R. L. Duncan’s Paisano, another 335th Squadron ship, causing Paisano to stall in her propeller wash. Paisano’s tail section then struck Aunt Callie’s Baby’s right wing. Her tail separated at the waist section, she rolled over onto her back, and she crashed at Schönebeck. Nine killed in action.

title: Three Missions Without a Story
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Three Missions Without a Story
body: The report attributes the loss to the collision itself, not to flak or fighters; nothing about that day’s target defenses caused it. It was filed against a mission from which the group lost nothing else at all. Tavis's own combat record shows only two missions total, this one and Ruhland the day before, with nothing recorded after — the database does not say why, and there is nothing to be gained by guessing. What his own family said decades later, at his memorial in Upland, California, was that he brought his own crew home safely that day. Both things happened in the same formation, over the same target, within the same hour: nine men killed in a collision inside their own group, and a pilot who, whatever ended his combat flying two missions later, got his own crew back to England intact.

title: Three Missions Without a Story
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Three Missions Without a Story
body: The next morning, March 4, the target was nominally Ulm, though the day’s own mission record shows Ulm was never the point of the exercise: the primary target was a Messerschmitt components factory at Baumenheim, and Ulm’s marshalling yard was the fallback, used only because cloud cover — ten-tenths undercast — closed out the primary. Crews were woken at 0215 for a 0315 briefing that day, airborne by 0600 in the dark, and the 95th Bomb Group flew it as the second group in its own wing’s formation, the 100th leading despite Horham’s status as the 13th Combat Bombardment Wing’s own headquarters. Being the wing’s home base did not mean flying first.

title: Three Missions Without a Story
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Three Missions Without a Story
body: Six days later, March 10, the crew flew again, to a target the record gives as Dortmunderfeld, in the same industrial corridor the Eighth had been working since Chemnitz.

title: Three Missions Without a Story
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Three Missions Without a Story
body: Ulm and Dortmunderfeld have neither a clipping nor a photograph. Brunswick has a print in the album, two ships in flak, marked in the family’s hand. They exist otherwise as lines in a database that does not explain itself, sitting quietly between a mission the family kept a newspaper page about and one that has already taken several pages here. That asymmetry is not a judgment on which missions mattered. It is a record of which ones a family, sixteen and eighteen and twenty-two years old at the time, happened to be handed a newspaper for — and which print they kept.

title: Swinemünde, March 12
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Swinemünde, March 12
body: Mission thirteen requires more care than any other in the record.

title: Swinemünde, March 12
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Swinemünde, March 12
body: The target was the German naval base at Swinemünde, on the Baltic, where reconnaissance had identified the pocket battleship Admiral Scheer and other naval vessels at anchor. The raid had been requested specifically by Soviet command, whose forces were closing on the area from the east. The 95th Bomb Group flew it as part of a larger Eighth Air Force effort; the family’s clipping — “Heavies Hit Near Rhine, Along Baltic” — records it from the American side, as one raid among the day’s operations.

title: Swinemünde, March 12
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Swinemünde, March 12
body: What the clipping does not record, and what the historical record surrounding Swinemünde makes unavoidable, is that the city’s population had grown enormously in the weeks before the raid with civilian refugees fleeing the advancing Eastern Front — families, mostly, moving west and north ahead of the Soviet advance, gathered in a port town that was, that week, also a legitimate naval target. Postwar accounts of civilian casualties at Swinemünde vary very widely, from the low thousands into the tens of thousands, and the sourcing behind the highest estimates deserves real skepticism about its framing and its agenda. What can be stated with confidence is this: a naval target, requested by an allied power, struck as ordered, in a city whose civilian population that week was far larger than its military significance alone would suggest, with a human cost that the surviving record does not allow anyone to state precisely.

title: Swinemünde, March 12
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Swinemünde, March 12
body: Frank Calicura’s crew flew the mission and came home. Nothing in the family’s own record indicates what, if anything, he understood about the civilians below him that day.

title: Seelze, March 14
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Seelze, March 14
body: Mission fourteen went to Seelze, west of Hannover, and it was among the roughest days the group had that spring. The 95th dispatched thirty-eight aircraft. Sixteen came back damaged, one was lost, and one more was written off after landing. Frank Calicura flew the Spirit of Martinez, call sign E, and brought her home.

title: Seelze, March 14
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Seelze, March 14
body: Another 335th Squadron crew did not have that day. G. E. Brumbaugh, flying 44-8438, was hit over the target, lost the number three propeller to a runaway and the number four engine to half power, and fell out of contact with the formation. Flak found the aircraft again near Frankfurt. The crew force-landed in Belgium. The report records eight men returned to duty, one wounded, and the aircraft salvaged.

title: Seelze, March 14
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Seelze, March 14
body: Sixteen damaged out of thirty-eight is a proportion the flight record does not register in any way. The individual flight record for March gives hours, not odds.

title: Seelze, March 14
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Seelze, March 14
body: The chart for the day survives in the family collection. It is a printed Newcastle-to-Prague sheet, annotated by hand, numbered fourteen and dated 14 March 1945, with four control points, an initial point and a rally point drawn around a target lettered Seelze.

title: Jena, March 19
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Jena, March 19
body: Mission fifteen was Jena, five days later, bombed through cloud along with Plauen. The family’s clipping is “Plane Plants, Airfields Struck By 1,200 Heavies.” What makes it worth more than its position in the sequence is what the escort ran into. Six hundred Mustangs engaged thirty-nine German aircraft that day, five of them jets — and not only the Me 262s that had been appearing since Munich, but Arado 234s, a jet bomber rather than a jet fighter, and a type the crews had not met before. The same raid struck a jet-parts factory at Baumenheim and airfields near Ingolstadt and Ulm believed to be assembling them.

title: Jena, March 19
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours Jena, March 19
body: Six weeks earlier the crew had flown their first mission in an aircraft designed in 1935. The war they were finishing in was not the one they had started.

title: What the Log Doesn’t Say
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours What the Log Doesn’t Say
body: By the end of the run that had started at Chemnitz and passed through Munich and Swinemünde, Frank Calicura had flown thirteen missions in twenty-seven days.

title: What the Log Doesn’t Say
titleText: Ninety-Four Hours What the Log Doesn’t Say
body: The flight record states the hours. It does not state what a man carried home from Swinemünde specifically, or from any of the twelve missions around it. That absence is not a failure of the archive. It is the ordinary condition of the record a mission generates — times, targets, tonnage, losses — set against everything a mission actually cost the nine men who flew it, which was never the kind of thing paperwork was built to hold.

title: Hamburg, March 20
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Hamburg, March 20
body: The chapter that follows is about the break in that pattern, and about the airplane that carried their town’s name.

title: Hamburg, March 20
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Hamburg, March 20
body: Mission sixteen was Hamburg, and the target was the Blohm+Voss shipyards — U-boat construction, still a priority target this late in the war because the submarine threat, though diminished, had not been eliminated. The family’s clipping, “Heavies Hit U-Boat Works,” matches the target. An aerial photograph in the collection shows smoke rising over the yards, the kind of image the Eighth Air Force produced by the thousands that spring to document what a mission had or had not accomplished.

title: Ahlhorn, March 22
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Ahlhorn, March 22
body: Two days later, mission seventeen struck the Luftwaffe airfield at Ahlhorn. That is where the crew record puts him. The family’s clipping kept against that page — “Few Enemy Planes Up, 22 KO’d” — names Ingolstadt, Fürth and Grafenwöhr, not Ahlhorn. The two records disagree. They are left in disagreement.

title: Ahlhorn, March 22
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Ahlhorn, March 22
body: Fields like Ahlhorn had begun to host the first operational jet aircraft, the Me 262 and the Arado 234. Bomber crews at this stage mostly heard about jet encounters rather than fought them. The aircraft were too fast and too few to intercept a bomber stream in numbers that mattered.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: Between Ahlhorn and the week the Spirit went down for her engine change, the crew record shows six more missions.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: March 23, Unna, the eighteenth. A dispatch on the Ruhr names the Unna-Dortmund yards among a dozen other targets.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: March 24, Ziegenhain. The scrapbook page has not been found. A number in the sequence, and nothing else.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: March 28, Hannover. The clipping is “1,250 Heavies Strike Tank, Gun Factories Near Hanover,” describing two tank plants and a factory making half-tracks hit in the city and at Hildesheim, with oil refineries at Misburg and Nienhagen and E-boat pens at Ijmuiden on the Dutch coast.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: March 31, Zeitz. The scrapbook page has not been found. A wire report recovered from a newspaper archive rather than from the family records the raid on the synthetic oil plant alongside Brandenburg, Brunswick and the Halle freight yards.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: April 3, Kiel, the first of two consecutive days.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: April 4, Kiel again. The clipping is “Heavies Rock Kiel for 2nd Day, Pound Hamburg and Airfields,” which reports nine bombers and four fighters lost across the Eighth Air Force that day, and fifteen German aircraft claimed by escorting fighters, eleven of them jets.

title: Six Missions Before the Break
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Six Missions Before the Break
body: No photograph, no letter, no mark of any kind setting any of the thinner mornings apart. They are dates in a run that, by early April, had gone on long enough that not every mission could be a story worth telling.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: Martinez earned the right to name a bomber the way war bond drives usually earned such things: by exceeding a quota. The city put up eight hundred fifty-five thousand dollars toward its Sixth War Loan Drive target and doubled it, and the aircraft assigned in return was 44-6838, formally christened Spirit of Martinez in a ceremony that came well after the fact — by the time Frank stood under the nose for the photograph, with Col. Jack Shuck and Capt. David Olsson beside him, the crew had already flown the ship nine times under the name themselves. The Army caught up to what the men had already decided to call her. Olsson’s presence in that photograph was not simply official; the caption the family kept notes him as another Martinez man, standing in a field in Suffolk under a nose someone from his own town had painted.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: The Gazette put the name in type on February 22 — the same morning as Bamberg. Martinez Puts Name on Plane. War Finance Chairman Ray Taylor had received word from W. W. Crocker that a Superfortress had been provided through the last bond campaign. That is the B-29, not 44-6838. Several weeks earlier Taylor had addressed a public letter to Lieutenant Calicura. The paper still puts Sam at 515 Mellus. Training finished two months ago. The handshake under the nose came after nine missions. This is the hometown announcement of a name the crew had already decided to use.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: A retrospective feature published decades later in the News-Gazette, built on an interview with Joyce, fills in how the name reached Frank in the first place. That article is used carefully here and in Chapter 13. Its handling of the operational record is unreliable — it misstates where Frank formed his crew, inflates both his mission count and the aircraft’s, and describes him in 1944 as the father of two when his first son was two months old — and every such figure in this book comes from the orders and crew records instead. What the article carries that nothing else does is Joyce’s own memory of things she was present for, and the committee’s correspondence, which she kept. A widow’s account of what her husband told her about the day he landed is a different kind of evidence from a reporter’s grasp of how many missions he flew, and it is treated differently here. The surplus from the bond drive was meant to buy a B-29 to carry the city’s name; the War Finance Committee, chaired by Ray S. Taylor, learned instead that a newly commissioned local pilot was forming a crew, and wrote to him directly. The committee’s letter is quoted: “We learn from one of your brothers that you and your crew have completed all training and are awaiting assignment of a B-17.” Somebody, the letter went on, had suggested it would be wonderful if the city had one of its own boys piloting a ship bearing its name, “so it could watch the ship’s exploits with pride and hope and feel true community kinship with the pilot, ship and crew.” Frank agreed. When the aircraft was delivered, the article states, he and the crew chose the name themselves — which is consistent with the nine missions they flew under it before the Army held its ceremony.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: The letter itself is in the collection. Addressed to Lieut. Frank Calicura, USA, somewhere in the Eastern U.S., awaiting assignment, and signed by the Martinez War Finance Committee and the Citizens of Martinez. The Sixth War Loan Drive had overrun an $815,000 quota; the Treasury said another $350,000 would buy a B-17 named City of Martinez. The paper asked him to put that name on his ship, and to let the town adopt “the whole ten or eleven of you.” This book has already carried $855,000 from a later account. The letter says $815,000. The paper asked for City of Martinez. The men painted Spirit. Eleven is the hometown paper’s crew, here as it was on the East Coast clipping.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: One detail in that account sits oddly against the photograph. The committee, the article reports, was disappointed to learn that the “name” consisted not of nose art “big enough for enemies to read without their glasses” but merely a small plaque mounted under the instrument panel. The surviving photograph of Frank beside the aircraft shows the name painted across the nose in script a good deal larger than a plaque. Both may be true in sequence — a plaque first, paint later, once the crew had adopted the name in earnest — but no document in the collection dates the painting, and the two accounts are not reconciled here.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: Frank’s own account of the honor, written to Ray Taylor a week before the engine change grounded the ship, reverses the direction the ceremony photograph suggests. “We should be the honored ones,” he wrote, “in having the people at home asking us to name it after our town.”

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: He wrote to Taylor about the airplane itself in the same register, and the boast he allowed himself was a narrow one. “We can brag about her, Ray,” he wrote. “In all those missions; not once did we or those others who were fortunate to fly her have to turn back; abort as we call it.” Not that she was lucky, or that the crew was — that the ship had never once failed to reach a target she was sent to.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: A published B-17 log, Dave Osborne’s Fortress Master Log, lists the same serial under another name: CAL'S RASCALS aka THE SPIRIT OF MARTINEZ. The Imperial War Museums’ American Archive repeats it. Neither is a wartime paper. The name on the nose, on the wallets, and in Frank’s letter to Ray Taylor is Spirit of Martinez. Cal’s Rascals is the log’s other name for the tail number, not a second christening.

title: How the Name Got There
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft How the Name Got There
body: There is a fact underneath the name that the ceremony had no way of marking. The town Frank Calicura was flying a bomber for had no airfield at all until 1939, when his own eldest brother helped drag one out of the waterfront fill, trucked in a hangar, and taught him to fly on it. Sam Calicura Jr. was thirty-six in 1942, a decade past the ceiling for aviation cadet training and born in Italy besides. He did not fly this war. The two brothers he had taught did.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: For twenty-three missions, Frank Calicura’s crew flew the same aircraft. On the twenty-fourth, they did not.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: The traffic ran the other way as well, and more often than this book first reported. On March 17, 1945, on a mission to Ruhland, the Spirit of Martinez flew to Germany without any of the nine men who thought of her as theirs. The crew record puts John Bradley’s crew in her that day — the same crew that had lent Frank Calicura a co-pilot on his first morning — while Frank’s own crew did not fly at all. An aircraft in good order did not sit on the ground because the men usually in it were resting.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: A second such day has since come to light, and it is not quite the same shape. On March 2, 1945, also to Ruhland, the Spirit flew under J.J. Getchius’s crew — but with Victor Probst, Frank’s own co-pilot, in the right-hand seat. The airplane went without her pilot and with one of her own men aboard. Frank did not fly that day at all.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: Whether the group flew two Ruhland missions that month, or whether one of these two dates is an error in a database compiled decades afterward, this book cannot establish. Both entries exist in the same record. Both are reported here.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: There is a third day, and it is the mirror of the first morning. On March 10, 1945, to Dortmunderfeld, Victor Probst flew with C.D. Crawford’s crew in 43-38255, Poof Proof, while the Spirit went out with Claude C. Greear in the right-hand seat — Crawford’s regular co-pilot, on the first mission of his life. In February a veteran had been placed beside a new pilot and Probst sent away to make room. In March the arrangement ran backwards: Probst was now the experienced man, and it was Frank’s airplane that took the stranger. The two co-pilots changed seats for one morning and changed back. Why is not recorded anywhere this writer has found, and nothing is gained by supposing.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: These three mornings account for a number that does not otherwise fit. The 95th Bomb Group’s database credits Probst with thirty-two sorties. The crew flew thirty-one. Twenty-nine of Probst’s were with Frank Calicura; three were not — Chemnitz with Bradley, Ruhland with Getchius, Dortmunderfeld with Crawford. Two men sat side by side for almost an entire tour and do not agree on how many times they flew, and neither of them is wrong. Thirty-two is the database’s figure, and appears in no wartime document held by this family.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: Joyce Calicura remembered him talking about this. Frank said the crew worried every time the back-up crew took her out, she told a reporter decades later, until she came back. The crew record supplies the date he was worrying about.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: The 95th Bomb Group’s crew record shows a break in the pattern on April 5, a mission to Nuremberg: the aircraft listed is not 44-6838, Spirit of Martinez, but 44-8269, a B-17 named The Red Fox.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: Two days later, on April 7, a mission to Kaltenkirchen shows a third aircraft again — 43-38942, Belligerent Beauty. The group’s compilation puts Donald J. Wilcox in the ball turret that morning, not Robert E. Collins, and Floyd L. Mathis aboard as observer.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: By April 9, on the mission to München-Riem, the crew was back in the Spirit. Wilcox again in the ball; Mathis still observing. Collins is not on that roster either. That mission has its own clipping in the collection — the companion to the Munich piece from February, and the one that actually belongs here: “1,250 Heavies Strike Munich,” describing more than 1,250 Fortresses and Liberators, protected by some 750 fighters, hammering ten airfields in the vicinity of the city, all of them believed to be bases for the jet-propelled fighters that had become the bomber force’s greatest source of trouble in recent weeks. It was the third straight day the Eighth had put more than a thousand bombers in the air, and the third day of a run that had by then hit twenty-seven airfields. Frank Calicura’s crew, flying the Spirit again for the first time since the engine change, took part in the kind of mission the closing weeks of the air war had become: not cities anymore, but the airfields the Luftwaffe’s last serious aircraft flew from.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: Frank’s own account, in a letter written from England on April 21, 1945, to a friend named Ray Taylor and later published under the title “If the People at Home Only Knew,” explains the gap without meaning to. He wrote that the Spirit had been stood down for an engine change — her third — after nearly fifty combat missions and more than four hundred combat hours. The dates align exactly: an aircraft flown that hard, pulled for maintenance in the first week of April, would put a crew into whatever airplane was available for a mission or two before their own ship came back on the line. Frank Calicura flew two combat missions in airplanes that were not his, in a week when the machine he trusted was somewhere on the ground at Horham with her cowlings off, and then he went back to her.

title: The Other Airplane
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Other Airplane
body: This is very likely the origin of a number the family has carried without fully being able to explain: thirty bomb symbols painted on the B-15 flight jacket in the collection, against a total logged count of twenty-eight combat missions and three humanitarian ones, thirty-one in all. Subtract the two missions flown in borrowed aircraft — April 5 in The Red Fox, April 7 in Belligerent Beauty — and the 95th Bomb Group’s own crew record puts the number flown specifically in the Spirit of Martinez at twenty-nine, not thirty. The jacket and the database disagree by exactly one symbol. It may be an extra mission the crew record simply doesn’t carry under 44-6838’s tail number, a training or ferry flight painted on alongside the combat count, or a man who miscounted his own jacket by one bomb in a hangar in England. What the arithmetic confirms is the shape of the count itself: a tally kept of an airplane rather than a man, accurate to within a single bomb.

title: Burg, April 10
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Burg, April 10
body: Mission twenty-seven was the next morning. The crew was back in the Spirit. The target was Burg — one of seven jet airfields in the arc around Berlin named in the clipping Joyce kept. The crew record puts him there on April 10. The scrapbook writes the same name in the margin. Wilcox still in the ball; George F. Gearn observing. Collins is not on this roster either.

title: Burg, April 10
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Burg, April 10
body: Nothing else in the collection marks the morning. No letter. No photograph. A number, a field, and a clipping that names it among others. The compilation names the seats. It does not say why Collins was missing those three days, or why he is back on the roster for Oranienburg ten days later.

title: Oranienburg, April 20
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Oranienburg, April 20
body: Mission twenty-eight, April 20, 1945. Rail yards ringing Berlin. The crew record’s last combat entry for this crew names Oranienburg. The scrapbook stops on the same date, the same target.

title: Oranienburg, April 20
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft Oranienburg, April 20
body: Ten days after Burg. Joyce numbered it Mission #28 in pencil. The three mornings over Utrecht that followed carry no number at all.

title: The Rest Center
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Rest Center
body: Sometime in this stretch — the collection dates it only broadly to the spring — Frank Calicura’s crew was sent to one of the Eighth Air Force’s rest homes for a week.

title: The Rest Center
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Rest Center
body: The system was real and specific: roughly twenty houses and hotels requisitioned across England, jointly run by Air Service Command and the American Red Cross, offering aircrew a week away from the base with no return home possible. Rank did not apply there. Men were issued civilian clothes for the stay, with uniforms required again only for dinner. It was, by design, as unmilitary an experience as the Army Air Forces could construct for men who had spent months being nothing else.

title: The Rest Center
titleText: Borrowed Aircraft The Rest Center
body: The family’s clipping records it plainly: “Spirit of Martinez Crew Takes Rest.” It is one of the only points in this entire chronology where the record shows the war stopping, briefly, rather than continuing.

title: Nine Wallets
titleText: Utrecht Nine Wallets
body: Sometime in the last weeks of the war in Europe, a carton arrived at Horham from the Martinez Kiwanis Club.

title: Nine Wallets
titleText: Utrecht Nine Wallets
body: Inside were nine wallets — good leather, the kind that had not been available on the retail market in America since 1942, each one stamped along the inside edge with SPIRIT OF MARTINEZ and, beneath it, a crew member’s own name. The club had ordered them that spring, thinking of the Pacific. With Germany’s collapse plainly imminent by April 1945, the assumption at home, reasonable enough at the time, was that the war these nine men had been fighting would simply relocate to the other side of the world, and that whatever the town could still send them was likely to matter for a while yet.

title: Nine Wallets
titleText: Utrecht Nine Wallets
body: Frank Calicura moved his cards into his that week — license, discharge papers to come, Joyce’s photograph, a stiff little card from a Soho club that could not be resold. He put the old wallet, worn soft against his thigh through twenty-eight missions, into the footlocker. The tags that went with him still give the enlisted serial, 19149763, and Joyce as Mrs. J. B. Calicura at 731 Mellus Street. They sit on the same clipping.

title: Nine Wallets
titleText: Utrecht Nine Wallets
body: Nobody in Martinez knew yet what these nine men were actually about to do instead.

title: The Hunger Winter
titleText: Utrecht The Hunger Winter
body: The crisis had begun the previous September, when the Dutch government-in-exile called a national railway strike to support the Allied advance during Operation Market Garden. The German occupying authorities retaliated by cutting food and fuel shipments to the country’s western provinces — Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, Utrecht — precisely the densely populated cities that depended on those shipments to survive. An unusually severe winter arrived on top of the embargo, and flooded agricultural land, deliberately inundated by the retreating German army, took much of the region’s remaining food production out of use entirely.

title: The Hunger Winter
titleText: Utrecht The Hunger Winter
body: By the winter of 1944–45, daily rations in the affected cities had fallen to somewhere between four hundred and five hundred calories — bread stretched with sugar beet pulp, soup made from boiled tulip bulbs, whatever could be found. A survivor named John Papenhuyzen, whose account is preserved by an oral history project dedicated to this operation, described the bread of that winter as bread in name only: made from beans, or from the syrup boiled down from sugar beets, spread thin because there was nothing to spread it thick with. Audrey Hepburn, a teenager in Arnhem that winter and among those later fed by the operation this chapter describes, remembered going as long as three days without food and living for months on “hot water and one slice of bread, made from brown beans.” An estimated three million Dutch civilians were living under these conditions. By the time the crisis ended, somewhere between eighteen and twenty-two thousand of them had died of it — the exact figure is still debated, but the order of magnitude is not.

title: The Truce
titleText: Utrecht The Truce
body: No one in a position to authorize a rescue actually had the authority to negotiate one directly.

title: The Truce
titleText: Utrecht The Truce
body: Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands appealed to the Allied command on his country’s behalf. General Eisenhower, sympathetic, did not have standing to negotiate a ceasefire with an enemy that had not surrendered. The solution came through Air Commodore Andrew Geddes, who met with German officers under General Johannes Blaskowitz and secured an informal understanding: Allied aircraft would fly low, unarmed corridors over designated drop zones, and German anti-aircraft crews — still very much in a position to shoot them down — would hold their fire. Nothing about the arrangement was formalized in the way a proper armistice would have been. It rested entirely on both sides keeping a word given under conditions where either could easily have broken it.

title: The Truce
titleText: Utrecht The Truce
body: The Royal Air Force began first, on April 29, in an operation it called Manna. The Americans followed on May 1 with Operation Chowhound, delayed at the very start by fog closing the English airfields. Together, before the war in Europe ended a week later, the two air forces flew something on the order of 5,500 sorties and delivered close to 10,000 tons of food. The Americans alone, in Chowhound, flew roughly 2,268 sorties and dropped approximately 4,000 tons — at an altitude of about four hundred feet and a speed of 150 to 175 knots, a combination that would have been suicidal in a contested airspace and was, over Holland that week, deliberately routine. Three American aircraft were lost during the operation: two in a mid-air collision, one to engine fire. None to enemy action. The Germans, for the most part, kept their word.

title: The Truce
titleText: Utrecht The Truce
body: Independent confirmation of the operation's scale survives outside the family's own collection as well. A wire photograph captioned "Manna from Heaven for the Dutch," showing a 385th Bomb Group Fortress — a different group from Frank's own, over a different Dutch city — running the same kind of low pass, reported that on each of the first three days of May, something on the order of four hundred B-17s a day dropped eight hundred tons of food toward drop zones the Dutch had marked and the airmen had pinpointed. It is not a family document. It ran in the general press, credited to the Army Air Force's own photographers, and it says nothing about Utrecht, the 95th, or any of the three mornings Frank Calicura's crew flew. What it confirms is only the scale and the choreography — hundreds of heavy bombers a day, flying low and slow over marked ground, at the precision the operation required — reported nationally while the missions themselves were still underway.

title: The Third, the Fourth, the Fifth
titleText: Utrecht The Third, the Fourth, the Fifth
body: Frank Calicura’s crew flew three of these missions: May 3, May 5, and May 6. All three were drops over Utrecht, at a place called Lage Weide.

title: The Third, the Fourth, the Fifth
titleText: Utrecht The Third, the Fourth, the Fifth
body: Nothing about the flying resembled what they had spent the previous three months doing. There was no formation to hold at altitude, no flak to climb through, no fighters to watch for. The bomb bay, built to carry explosives, carried food instead — flour, tinned meat, chocolate, powdered milk, packed and released at a height low enough that the crew could see, clearly, the people the cargo was landing among. Dutch civilians had learned within days to mark the fields with sheets, and to stand in the open where the aircraft could see them, in a way no one stands in the open during a war unless they have decided the war has, for this airplane, stopped applying to them.

title: The Third, the Fourth, the Fifth
titleText: Utrecht The Third, the Fourth, the Fifth
body: The operation was numbered sequentially by the group — Chowhound One, Two, and so on — and Frank’s crew flew the third mission of that sequence, then the fourth two days later, then the fifth the day after that. They had not flown the operation’s opening days. By the time their names went up on the board for it, the arrangement had already held for two days without incident. An agreement between enemies, tested and so far unbroken, before the third crew from the 95th Bomb Group’s own record ever got their turn to trust it.

title: What They Found There
titleText: Utrecht What They Found There
body: An unnamed account, posted online years later alongside photographs of the drops, recalls a relative who was a child in Holland that spring, and who remembered — the family’s own words — that the white bread tasted like cake.

title: What They Found There
titleText: Utrecht What They Found There
body: This detail cannot be verified to a name, a date, or a specific drop zone, and it should not be read as documented fact in the way the mission dates and tonnage above are documented. What can be said is that it matches, almost exactly, what named survivors of that winter did say about the food that fell out of the sky in May 1945. Bread made from brown beans, bread stretched with beet pulp, soup boiled from tulip bulbs — and then, after months of that, bread made from wheat, the way bread was supposed to be made. To a child who had not tasted it in the better part of a year, there is no particular reason to doubt that it tasted like cake. The reaction she is remembered as having had was, by every documented account of that winter, the ordinary one.

title: What They Found There
titleText: Utrecht What They Found There
body: Frank Calicura flew three missions into that reception and never described, in any surviving letter, what it looked like from four hundred feet. The collection kept the view anyway: the mill on the approach, the doors open, the white sacks on the field.

title: What They Found There
titleText: Utrecht What They Found There
body: The nine wallets in the footlocker, stamped for a war in the Pacific that never came, are still the artifact of the days just before it — nine men expecting one thing, and being handed, instead, three mornings over Utrecht that had nothing to do with what any of them had trained for.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: The Spirit of Martinez left England for the last time on June 21, 1945, landing at Bradley Field, Connecticut, with the crew that had flown her through the final months of the war in Europe. Frank Calicura came home a first lieutenant with a War Department tally-out receipt for his sidearm and ammunition, a pay and allowance voucher, and a Certificate of Service that reduced two and a half years to a handful of dates and a rank.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: That certificate survives in the collection, and it says considerably more than the summary above allows. It gives his rank at separation as First Lieutenant, Air Corps, Army of the United States, serial number 0-828662; his civilian occupation as butcher and meatcutter; and his military occupational specialty as Pilot (1091). It credits him with three battle stars — Central Europe, Ardennes, and Western Europe — the first two by official Army certificate and the third by his own official claim, a distinction the form itself preserves without explaining further. None of the three appears elsewhere in this book. It records his departure from the continental United States on December 18, 1944, and his arrival in England on January 6, 1945 — the date already corrected in Chapters 7 and 8, where this book had previously given, without a document behind it, the first of the month.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: The certificate also documents a stretch of Frank Calicura's service this book had not, until now, been able to account for at all. His organization at the time of separation was not the 95th Bomb Group but the 207th AAF Base Unit, Deming Army Air Field, New Mexico — a stateside posting that placed him roughly two thousand miles from Martinez for some part of the five months between his return to the United States on June 21, 1945, and his relief from active duty on November 12, 1945.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: A transfer order fills in one piece of that gap. Special Orders Number 75, Headquarters Sioux Falls Army Air Field, Sioux Falls, South Dakota, dated 14 August 1945, releases First Lieutenant Frank J. Calicura, serial 0828662, from assignment to the 335th Bomb Squadron, 95th Bomb Group — his own combat squadron, still carried as his organization of record more than seven weeks after he had left England — and transfers him in grade to Deming Army Air Field, New Mexico, with property, on or about August 16, 1945, to report there for duty (family collection). The order places him at Sioux Falls sometime before mid-August, a stop this book has not otherwise documented, and it is the first direct evidence of how he actually got from the East Coast to New Mexico: not directly, but by way of South Dakota. What he did at either stop, and how long he had been at Sioux Falls before the transfer, go unrecorded. Separation itself was processed closer to home, at March Field, California, but still not in Martinez. Frank's own signature closes the separation form; John M. Guthrie, Second Lieutenant, Air Corps, signed as the officer supervising his separation.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: One further document closes out the paper trail nearly two years later. On April 17, 1947, the War Department's Adjutant General's Office sent Frank — along with, by the letter's own address line, every other officer who had served in the war — a form letter over the signature of Major General Edward F. Witsell, forwarding a commission in the highest rank he had attained. The letter is explicit that this did not constitute a new appointment, only formal evidence of a rank already earned, "forwarded to you with the grateful thanks and deep appreciation of the War Department for your services." It is the last document from the Army anywhere in this collection.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: What happened to the aircraft on landing is recorded only in Joyce’s own account, given decades later. Ray Taylor and other Martinez men had tried to reach Eighth Air Force commander Jimmy Doolittle through his peacetime employer, Shell Oil, hoping the ship could be brought somewhere townspeople could see her. The War Department had other plans. “The saddest part Frank said, was when he had to fly it back,” Joyce told the News-Gazette. “When he landed, before he got his stuff off, they had dismantled it and towed it away. He said if he had known, he would have gotten souvenirs.” By the time the Chamber of Commerce and the town’s service clubs held a luncheon at Armando’s to honor Frank and the other returning servicemen — a dollar twenty-five a plate, with a fountain pen presented to him in appreciation of the city’s obligation for naming his ship after it — the airplane the luncheon was partly about had already been broken up.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: The aircraft did not come home with him for long. She went on to South Plains, Texas, that same summer, and was sold for scrap at Kingman, Arizona, on December 19, 1945 — six months after carrying Frank Calicura across the Atlantic for the last time, and not quite eleven months after she had first been assigned to his squadron. The 95th Bomb Group itself, which had flown from Horham for the whole of Frank’s combat tour and most of two years before it, is credited with something on the order of three hundred and twenty combat missions from that airfield — the exact figure varies by a few missions depending on which record is consulted, which is itself consistent with everything else the record shows about how bomb groups counted their own history.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: Frank returned to Martinez, to Joyce, to a son he had a photograph of before he had held him, and eventually to a butcher’s apron and a shop on Main Street with his brother Bill. He also returned with a commercial pilot’s rating and an instructor’s endorsement, recommended in writing by the last man to command the group he had flown with. The field where he had first been taught to fly was still shut, requisitioned out of civilian use since 1941. His brother was already working to get it back.

title: Home
titleText: What Came Back Home
body: The pay and allowance voucher survives as an actual card, dated June 15, 1945 — six days before the Spirit left England for the last time — and it reduces the return itself to the same arithmetic that had governed everything before it. Base pay and longevity, $183.33. Flying pay, $91.67. Rental allowance, $75.00. Subsistence, $42.00. A total of $392.00 a month, a $200 allotment, $6.60 in insurance, a deduction for field rations. Joyce B. Calicura is listed as a dependent at 731 Mellus Street; beneath her, a second line notes that evidence of dependency for his mother had been filed under a separate voucher, a second claim on the same pay working through the system on its own schedule. It is not a different kind of document from the shipping ticket that itemized his flying gear by part number, or the memorandum that itemized his missions by general order. It is the same clerical habit turned toward the same man at the other end of the war: everything about Frank Calicura the Army thought worth recording, it recorded as a number.

title: March 2, 1946
titleText: What Came Back March 2, 1946
body: This is a correction to an earlier stage of the research. The family’s collection dates his death to December 7, 1945 — the fourth anniversary of Pearl Harbor — and an earlier draft of this chapter built directly on that date, reading a meaning into it that the actual record does not support.
