Cemetery burial records, sourced independently of the family’s own compilation, give the correct date as March 2, 1946, and a photograph of the Martinez News-Gazette’s edition from that same day is preserved alongside the record. The collection’s December date appears to be simply mistaken — the kind of error found in that same compilation before, corrected before, and corrected again here.

title: March 2, 1946
titleText: What Came Back March 2, 1946
body: There is no anniversary to make of March 2, 1946. It was, as far as the surviving record shows, an ordinary late-winter day.

title: March 2, 1946
titleText: What Came Back March 2, 1946
body: This is a second correction, and it goes the other direction from the first one. An earlier stage of the research assumed Sam Calicura Jr. died without seeing his brothers fly again. He did not. A Gazette article from early 1946 records the Martinez Airport reopening under lease to Sam Calicura and Charlie Beatie, its landing-area designation obtained from the CAA the week before, with Ralph Donohue of Martinez — recently released from the Navy — as a third partner. The field was limited to private fliers, with storage, repair, and a sales agency for a civilian airplane firm; no instruction this time, only operation. Sam Calicura’s three brothers, the paper noted, would run it with him: Frank, a first lieutenant discharged from the Army Air Corps, doing what flying the field required; Nick, out of the Navy Air Corps, in charge of repair; Bill, who had served in the Navy air corps’ ground forces, assisting both. That last description is the 1946 paper’s, and it does not match the wartime record set out in Chapter 4: an April 1944 Gazette item places Bill at Nashville, Tennessee, in the Army’s antiaircraft artillery, and his mother’s obituary that July calls him Corporal, a rank the Navy does not use. Two documents written during the war disagree with one written after it. The later paper is reproduced here as it stands, and the conflict is left open.

title: March 2, 1946
titleText: What Came Back March 2, 1946
body: Sam Calicura Jr. died a few weeks into that arrangement, not at the end of a long wait to see it, but in the middle of actually running it. He had built the field in 1939, watched the war take it away in 1941, and lived to reopen it in 1946 with three of his own brothers standing beside him — the same brothers he had taught to fly there in the first place. He is the reason any of them ever flew at all, and for a handful of weeks at the start of 1946, he got to watch it work exactly the way he must have once imagined it would.

title: March 2, 1946
titleText: What Came Back March 2, 1946
body: An independent source, found after this chapter was first drafted, confirms the date from outside the family’s own record entirely. A genealogical registry citing the California Death Index and the 1940 federal census gives Sam Calicura Jr.’s death as March 2, 1946, at Sunset View Cemetery in El Cerrito — the same date already established here through cemetery records and the Gazette’s own front page. The same source also supplies something the family’s collection had not: exact birth and death years for several of Sam’s siblings, most of them corroborating what this book already had — Nick (1908–2006), Dominic (1919–2008), Frank (1921–1962), William (1922–1986) — and one correction worth stating rather than absorbing silently. Antoinette, listed elsewhere in this book only as the Placerville aunt who took Jimmy Calicura in to work her family’s laundry business in 1963, appears here as Antoinette Florence Calicura Douvres, 1913–1996 — a daughter of Saverio and Angelina in her own right, not simply an in-law by marriage. She was already established in Placerville by the time of Sam’s death in 1946, seventeen years before her nephew arrived there. Jimmy’s move in 1963, in other words, was not a young man drifting to wherever work could be found. It was a family placement, an aunt taking in a brother’s son, in a town the family had already been living in for most of two decades.

title: March 2, 1946
titleText: What Came Back March 2, 1946
body: Two smaller discrepancies surfaced by the same source are noted rather than resolved. It gives Angelina’s birth year as 1884, four years earlier than the approximately 1888 this book has used, derived from a 1928 Gazette article that put her age at forty at her sixteenth child’s birth. It gives Virginia’s birth year as 1925 against this book’s existing 1926. Neither conflict is large enough to argue past a single source in either direction, and neither is resolved here.

title: March 2, 1946
titleText: What Came Back March 2, 1946
body: The field outlived him. A Contra Costa Gazette front page from April 1, 1947 — thirteen months after Sam’s death, its own headline given over to a missing Stinson and three men aboard — lists Charles Beatie as Martinez Airport’s manager and Ralph Donohue as his assistant, the same two men Sam had brought in as partners the year before, still running the place he had leased back into operation. A third name appears alongside them, new to the record: Lloyd Davis, a mechanic with his own garage business in Pleasant Hill. None of Sam’s brothers are mentioned. Whatever role Frank, Nick, and Bill had played in that first reopened season, by 1947 the field’s day-to-day operation belonged to Beatie and Donohue alone. That is not evidence the family had stepped away. A newspaper covering an aircraft in trouble near Quincy had no reason to name every man who worked the field, and did not.

title: Main Street, 1946–1955
titleText: What Came Back Main Street, 1946–1955
body: The record is silent on exactly what happened to the family’s meat business in the years immediately after Sam Calicura Jr.’s death. What can be established is the shape on either side of that gap, not the gap itself.

title: Main Street, 1946–1955
titleText: What Came Back Main Street, 1946–1955
body: By 1954, Frank and his brother Bill were running Calicura Bros. Meats out of space inside Martellacci’s grocery at Main and Castro, advertising rock cod, sliced bacon, hams, and steaks alongside Martellacci’s own produce and staples — a shared storefront, one family’s meat counter operating inside another’s store. The arrangement is dateable with some precision: a surviving flyer for a “Cupboard Sale” places Friday-Saturday specials on July 2–3 and a closure for July 4–5, a calendar pattern that matches 1954. Nothing in the collection documents when the Martellacci’s arrangement began, only that it was already running by then — leaving an undocumented stretch of roughly five years between Sam’s death in 1946 and the earliest date this book can independently confirm.

title: Main Street, 1946–1955
titleText: What Came Back Main Street, 1946–1955
body: On July 22, 1955, the Gazette covered what came next: Frank, thirty-five, and Bill, thirty-four, preparing to leave Martellacci’s for their own renovated quarters at 700 Main Street, opening shortly after August 1. The article states that the two brothers had operated out of Martellacci’s “for the past four years” — placing the start of that arrangement at approximately 1951, five years after Sam’s death, not immediately following it. It traces the business back further still: the family, it states, had been in the meat trade thirty years by 1955, dating to roughly 1925, consistent with what this book has already established about the Star Meat Market where Frank himself had worked as a young man. It also states that Frank and Bill had taken over the shop from their brother Sam “following his death in 1947.” That date conflicts with the one already established in this book — March 2, 1946, confirmed independently through cemetery records, contemporary Gazette coverage, and a genealogical registry — and the conflict is noted rather than resolved. A reporter working nine years after the fact, from memory or an uncertain source, is a plausible explanation; it is not a documented one.

title: Main Street, 1946–1955
titleText: What Came Back Main Street, 1946–1955
body: What the two dates agree on, regardless of which year is correct, is the sequence: Sam built the trade, died young, and his younger brothers carried it forward rather than letting it end with him. The “Thanks a million” notice that ran alongside the move, addressed to the shop’s customers and signed simply “Frank and Bill Calicura,” confirms the same expansion the article describes — a butcher’s counter growing into a store with a delicatessen, staples, and frozen foods, roughly a decade after Frank had come home from a war that had nothing to do with any of it.

title: Billy’s Horn
titleText: What Came Back Billy’s Horn
body: Billy Calicura played saxophone before he ever wore a butcher’s apron, and he did not stop when he put one on. A newspaper advertisement from the State Theater in Martinez, undated but placed by its own bill — a screening of “Meet Danny Wilson,” released in 1951 — to approximately that year, promotes a Friday-midnight “Jive Jam Session” on the theater’s stage: Russ Arno singing, Frank Meyers on bass, Benny Marcella at the piano, C. C. Pinkston on drums, and, billed with his own box on the page, “Billy Calicura and His Hot Sax.”

title: Billy’s Horn
titleText: What Came Back Billy’s Horn
body: Nothing else in the collection documents this side of Billy’s life in any detail — how often he played, how long the arrangement with the State Theater ran, or whether it continued once Calicura Bros. Meats took on its later shape. What the clipping confirms is narrower: the family’s musical thread, elsewhere carried by Frank’s trombone, ran through Billy as well, in public, on a marquee, in the same years he was learning the trade at his brothers’ side.

title: The Others
titleText: What Came Back The Others
body: The nine men who signed the same shipping ticket in December 1944 and flew the Spirit of Martinez through the final months of the war did not stay together afterward. What the record preserves of their later lives arrives mostly from outside the family’s own collection.

title: The Others
titleText: What Came Back The Others
body: John R. Barnes earned a doctorate at Penn State and spent much of his career as Director of Pathology at DuPont’s Haskell Laboratory, retiring in 1982. He died in Wellsboro, Pennsylvania, on June 2, 2011, at eighty-nine. A later compilation in the Imperial War Museums’ American Archive identifies him as navigator of the Spirit of Martinez; the biography on that page was supplied in part by his son. It is not a paper issued at Horham. Victor G. Probst returned to England to study architecture at the University of London, then co-founded a Texas firm that designed hospitals — Houston’s St. Luke’s and Texas Children’s among them. The same man who had spent 1945 in the nose of a B-17 spent the next three decades designing places built to keep people alive.

title: The Others
titleText: What Came Back The Others
body: Marvin L. Markus went home to Kingfisher, Oklahoma, married Dorothy Ellen O’Niel in July 1945 — a marriage that lasted sixty-nine years; she died December 16, 2014 — and built an automotive-electric business that expanded across several towns before he retired in 2003. He died March 30, 2015, at eighty-nine, and was buried at Kingfisher County Memorial Cemetery with full military rites. The Bartlesville Examiner-Enterprise obituary is the source of a number the family has carried: twenty-eight full bombing runs.

title: The Others
titleText: What Came Back The Others
body: Earle F. Bogacki stayed in uniform for thirty-one years, rising to Chief Master Sergeant and serving through Korea and Vietnam. He married Emily “Lu” McGrath on May 3, 1952, later delivered rural mail in Greenville, Pennsylvania, and died on February 14, 2011, at ninety, buried with full military honors. Her 2020 obituary names him and confirms the rank. Dale S. Ernest went to West Virginia University, then to the Naval Ordnance Laboratory in Silver Spring, Maryland, where by January 1959 he held a patent for an automatic depth-correcting device for moored mines. That same year he appears in the family’s own slide index — a visit, a supper, an evening on the back step — before eventually returning to Silver Spring for good. He died in 2007. Robert J. Brown married in Manhattan in December 1947; the license is the last documented trace of him found. James A. Titus’s later record remains thin beyond the wartime clippings already cited. Robert E. Collins’s later life is otherwise thin in the record beyond the draft card and the shipping ticket already cited — a name, a seat, three mornings he was not in it, and nothing after that the family has been able to follow.

title: The Others
titleText: What Came Back The Others
body: None of those later careers explains what the nine of them shared in a B-17 in 1945. The family kept what it kept — a visit, a name in a hospital firm, a patent clipped from a West Virginia paper — because it mattered enough to record.

titleText: What Came Back 1948
body: Three years after Frank came home, two sets of documents survive from the same year, and together they show a household still actively building rather than simply settled.

titleText: What Came Back 1948
body: Frank's own Second Class Airmen medical certificate, issued by the Civil Aeronautics Administration and examined July 7, 1948, at 731 Mellus Street, lists no limitations. It is a routine renewal, not a milestone, but it confirms directly what §13.1 had only inferred from the commercial pilot's rating and instructor's endorsement he brought home in 1945: three years on, Frank was still an active, medically certified civil airman, not simply a veteran carrying a wartime credential he no longer used.

titleText: What Came Back 1948
body: Joyce Calicura's own record from the same year documents something this book has not previously had occasion to record. On March 1, 1948, she was appointed Deputy Sheriff of Contra Costa County, badge number 72, under Sheriff James N. Long — a working appointment, not an honorary one, with her own signature and a right-index fingerprint on the reverse of the card. It expired January 2, 1951. Seven and a half months after that appointment, on October 15, 1948, the Federal Communications Commission issued her a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit at San Francisco, authorizing her to operate licensed radiotelephone stations under FCC rules and regulations.

titleText: What Came Back 1948
body: The collection does not state outright that the two credentials were connected — that the radio permit was obtained specifically for the deputy sheriff work, rather than for the family's continuing aviation activity, in which operating a station under FCC rule was an ordinary requirement of the era. Either explanation fits the timing equally well, and the collection does not choose between them.

titleText: What Came Back 1948
body: What is not in question is a role for Joyce Calicura this book has otherwise had no occasion to document. In 1948, while raising a young son, she held a county badge, a federal radio operator's license, and a fingerprint on file with the Contra Costa Sheriff's Office — three credentials that, together, describe a working woman rather than simply the dependent named on Frank's own wartime paperwork.

title: Seven Numbers
titleText: The Number Seven Numbers
body: Ask how many missions Frank Calicura flew, and the honest answer depends on which document is doing the counting.

title: Seven Numbers
titleText: The Number Seven Numbers
body: Twenty-six is the threshold of the Lucky Bastard Club, a squadron tradition rather than an official Army count, and the card in the family’s collection commemorates his membership in it. Twenty-eight is the number of combat missions the 95th Bomb Group’s own crew record shows him flying, from Chemnitz on February 14 to Oranienburg on April 20. Thirty is painted in bomb symbols on his flight jacket — not, as it turns out, his own mission total, and not quite the number of missions he flew specifically in 44-6838, the Spirit of Martinez herself, either. Subtracting the two missions flown in borrowed aircraft while she sat grounded for an engine change, the crew record accounts for twenty-nine of those thirty symbols and leaves the last one unexplained. Thirty-one is not a number any single document states, but it is the most complete count available once two of them are read together: Lieutenant Colonel Robert Stuart’s own memorandum, dated May 8, 1945, certifies twenty-eight operational missions and two hundred eight combat hours — the same crew-record figure already established here, put in writing by Frank’s own commanding officer at the very end of the group’s existence as a fighting unit — and the group’s separate mission log adds three humanitarian sorties over Utrecht that Stuart’s certification, concerned only with combat performance, does not count. Add them together and the total is thirty-one. Stuart’s memorandum alone still says twenty-eight. The group’s modern compiled crew record titles the listing F.J. Calicura, 31 — independently the same figure, and not a paper issued at Horham. Forty-eight appeared in a Public Forum letter to the Martinez Gazette, a hometown’s rounding-up of a hometown son’s service, generous rather than accurate. Nearly fifty was the figure Frank used himself, in April 1945, describing not his own tally but the Spirit’s — the number of combat missions she had flown, under whichever crew was assigned her, without a single abort. Fifty-three is where that number finally stopped, the aircraft’s full lifetime total from her first assignment through the end of the war, under every pilot who ever sat in her left seat.

title: Seven Numbers
titleText: The Number Seven Numbers
body: None of these seven numbers is a lie. Each answers a different question — a club’s rule, a squadron’s log, a jacket a man painted himself, a colonel’s judgment, a town’s affection, an airplane’s own life.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: After Frank Calicura came home, he and Joyce sat down and put the war in order.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: She had been collecting all along. Letters reached Martinez on no fixed schedule, and what the family relayed from them reached the Gazette on another; the local papers printed what they printed, when they printed it, and Joyce clipped as it appeared. What she could not do, while it was happening, was sequence it. The delay between a mission and its appearance in print was real and it varied, which meant the pile accumulated across a range of dates rather than in the order the missions were flown.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: The ordering came afterward, with Frank in the room. He supplied the dates, the photographs, the identification of which raid was which. She glued the pieces onto black pages and wrote a number in the margin of each one in pencil: Mission #1, Mission #6, Mission #14. The numbering runs from the middle of February 1945 to the third week of April, and it stops at twenty-eight.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: Set beside the 95th Bomb Group’s own operational record, the sequence matches mission for mission. The first is the Chemnitz raid of February 14; the second, Cottbus, the day after. Osnabrück is third, the two Nuremberg raids fourth and fifth. The sixth is the Stars and Stripes of Friday, February 23, reporting six thousand aircraft against the whole German rail network — a story that does not name Bamberg. Frank wrote it in the white margin in block capitals. The thirteenth is Swinemünde. The fourteenth names the marshalling yards at Seelze, the fifteenth the war plants at Jena, the seventeenth the airfield at Ahlhorn, the eighteenth the yards at Unna — the same four targets the crew record lists at those same four positions. The twenty-sixth is Munich, the twenty-seventh the attack on the jet airfields in the arc around Berlin — a story naming Burg among the seven fields struck, which is where the crew record puts him on April 10. The twenty-eighth, and last, is a raid on rail yards ringing Berlin whose target list ends with Oranienburg: April 20, 1945, the final combat mission of his war.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: The spread on the black page is that Friday paper, both columns, glued sideways. Mission #6 on the left. The right-hand column is the second Nuremberg, already numbered 5. One map in the same book circles Chemnitz and carries a number that may be 7 or 8. This book numbers Chemnitz first. The pencil is the thesis. It is not required to be tidy.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: What the match demonstrates is precise, and it is not corroboration. Lieutenant Colonel Robert H. Stuart certified twenty-eight operational missions at Horham on May 8, 1945, working from squadron paperwork. The scrapbook reaches twenty-eight because Frank Calicura, sitting in a kitchen in Martinez with a shoebox of clippings and his wife beside him, counted to twenty-eight. These are not two tallies that happen to agree. They are the Army’s count and the man’s own count, and the man’s own count is accurate — which is a smaller claim than independent confirmation and a more interesting one. He remembered his war correctly, in order, target by target, months after it ended.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: One number in the sequence settles what he thought he was counting. The twenty-fourth is the raid on the ordnance depots in southern Germany, the one whose rail targets included Nuremberg — April 5, 1945, the mission Frank Calicura flew in The Red Fox while the Spirit of Martinez sat at Horham with her cowlings off. It is numbered the same as the rest. This was not a record of an airplane. It was a record of a man, and the airplane he happened to be in that day did not change the count.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: What the numbering does not include is equally exact. The three Chowhound drops over Utrecht in May carry no number at all. He did not count them as missions — which is what the Army concluded as well, and which is why twenty-eight and thirty-one are both true statements about the same spring. He was counting the times he was sent somewhere people would shoot at him.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: The scrapbook does not settle the jacket. Thirty bomb symbols were painted on the B-15 in the footlocker; the count reaches twenty-eight combat missions, of which two were flown in borrowed aircraft, and three humanitarian drops go unnumbered. No arrangement of those figures produces thirty. That discrepancy stands where it stood.

title: Numbered in Pencil
titleText: The Number Numbered in Pencil
body: What the scrapbook settles is something the record could not show before. The clippings this book has drawn on for eleven chapters were not a scattering of what happened to survive. They are a series, assembled deliberately, by two people who had the whole thing behind them and decided it should be kept in order.

title: October 30, 1959
titleText: The Number October 30, 1959
body: The claim file preserves a sworn statement from a man who trained with Frank at Avon Park in the fall of 1944. He recalled, years later and for the record, that Frank had suffered a severe back condition sometime between September and November of that year — before either of them had flown a combat mission — bad enough that he needed help getting into and out of the aircraft.

title: October 30, 1959
titleText: The Number October 30, 1959
body: That is where the injury the Veterans Administration would spend fifteen years adjudicating actually began: not over Germany, but on a training field in Florida, months before the war Frank Calicura is remembered for had started for him at all.

title: October 30, 1959
titleText: The Number October 30, 1959
body: The VA’s decision arrived on October 30, 1959, under claim number C-1,302,621. Compensation was denied. The letter’s own language is more careful than the round number the family has carried forward: the condition was found either not service-connected, or service-connected but rated below the ten-percent threshold required for compensation. Both readings were available in the same sentence. Neither one was a simple no.

title: October 30, 1959
titleText: The Number October 30, 1959
body: Which of the two the examiner meant cannot be known, because the surviving letter does not say, and the ambiguity is better left unresolved than settled by preference. What can be said is narrower and, in its way, harder: a man who could not enter or exit an airplane without help in 1944 was told, fifteen years later, that the government could not establish what had caused it, or that whatever had caused it did not rise to the level the regulations required. The distinction mattered enormously to a claims examiner in Washington. It is not obvious that it mattered at all to the back.

title: The Ribbon Without a Citation
titleText: The Number The Ribbon Without a Citation
body: The service coat survives, and the ribbon bar is still mounted on it. Read left to right, in the order he wore it: a Distinguished Flying Cross in the first position, then the Air Medal carrying three oak leaf clusters, then the European-African-Middle Eastern Campaign Medal with its bronze service stars. Pilot wings above, the winged propeller of the Air Corps on the lapel. The headstone gives the shorter version — Air Medal, three oak leaf clusters. At least one archival summary of the service record, drawn from surviving discharge paperwork, is shorter still: it lists the Air Medal and its clusters, a Good Conduct Medal, the campaign medal, and the WWII Victory Medal, and does not mention a DFC at all.

title: The Ribbon Without a Citation
titleText: The Number The Ribbon Without a Citation
body: The Eighth Air Force awarded these decorations by a fixed formula, not by individual discretion: an Air Medal for every five qualifying combat sorties, an additional oak leaf cluster for every five beyond that, and — by a policy letter dated November 1942 — a Distinguished Flying Cross awarded in place of the fourth cluster, at the twenty-five-sortie mark. Run against Frank Calicura’s own record, the formula lands exactly where the headstone says it should: one Air Medal, three clusters, and at sortie twenty-five, a cross instead of a fourth ribbon. It is not four separate acts of individual valor. It is a ledger, kept automatically, translated into metal at fixed intervals.

title: The Ribbon Without a Citation
titleText: The Number The Ribbon Without a Citation
body: A memorandum in the family's collection, dated 8 May 1945 and signed by Lieutenant Colonel Robert H. Stuart, supplies what the surviving discharge paperwork does not: the citation numbers behind the ribbon itself. It credits First Lieutenant Frank J. Calicura with the Air Medal per General Order 289, 27 February 1945; a first oak leaf cluster per General Order 482, 15 March 1945; a second per General Order 638, 28 March 1945; and a third per General Order 720, 7 April 1945 — all issued by Headquarters, 3rd Air Division. It says nothing about a Distinguished Flying Cross, in either direction.

title: The Ribbon Without a Citation
titleText: The Number The Ribbon Without a Citation
body: Three of those four general orders survive in the collection as the orders themselves, not simply as Stuart's later summary of them. General Orders Number 289, Headquarters 3rd Air Division, 27 February 1945, lists Second Lieutenant Frank J. Calicura, serial 0828662, among the 95th Bombardment Group officers and enlisted men awarded the Air Medal — the same citation Stuart's memorandum would repeat ten weeks later. General Orders Number 638, 28 March 1945, and Number 720, 7 April 1945, both award him an Oak Leaf Cluster to that medal, both under the same serial number, both matching Stuart's later citation numbers exactly. Only General Orders Number 482, the first cluster, is not present in the collection; nothing here supplies it.

title: The Ribbon Without a Citation
titleText: The Number The Ribbon Without a Citation
body: The three surviving orders had already narrowed Frank Calicura's promotion to a six-week window — Second Lieutenant on the February 27 order, First Lieutenant by March 28. A fourth document fixes the date exactly. Special Orders Number 74, Headquarters Eighth Air Force, 15 March 1945, promotes Frank J. Calicura, serial 0828662, from Second to First Lieutenant, Army of the United States, with rank effective that same date — by command of Lieutenant General Doolittle, signed John S. Allard, Brigadier General, Chief of Staff (family collection). A contemporary hand has noted "Lt. Calicura, 335th" at the top of the page, confirming his squadron. The promotion landed almost exactly at the midpoint of the window the general orders had bracketed, nine days after his first Air Medal citation and thirteen days before his second oak leaf cluster — inside the same six-week stretch of his combat tour, and now dated to the day.

title: The Ribbon Without a Citation
titleText: The Number The Ribbon Without a Citation
body: The bar on that coat is not a description of an award. It is the award, mounted in precedence order by the man it was issued to, and a pilot does not put a Distinguished Flying Cross at the head of his own ribbon bar by accident. Set against it, the absence of a citation is easily explained without doubting the ribbon. The award required no individual narrative and no separate ceremony — it was a substitution within an existing sequence, processed as paperwork rather than granted as recognition. And a great deal of that paperwork no longer exists at all. In July 1973, a fire at the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis destroyed roughly eighty percent of Army personnel files for men discharged between 1912 and 1960, with no duplicates and no microfilm backup. For a very large number of World War II veterans, the individual service file simply does not survive to be checked. A missing citation, set against a ribbon still mounted on the coat, is not evidence the award was never made. It is the ordinary condition of a record that burned.

title: The Ribbon Without a Citation
titleText: The Number The Ribbon Without a Citation
body: Frank Calicura flew the twenty-five sorties the formula required. The ribbon, wherever its citation went, was earned by arithmetic before it was ever earned by anything the Army thought worth writing down.

title: The Footlocker
titleText: The Number The Footlocker
body: What remains, in a closet in California, is a box.

title: The Footlocker
titleText: The Number The Footlocker
body: A certificate honoring a Lucky Bastard’s twenty-six missions. A dollar bill signed by nine men and their families in a room nobody wrote an account of. A wallet stamped for a war that ended before it could be used for one. A jacket with thirty bomb symbols on it, some of them likely meant for missions that carried food instead of anything that could kill. A government letter, dated October 30, 1959, that could not quite decide whether a man’s back belonged to the government or not, and denied him either way. A ribbon whose citation may have burned in a fire in Missouri twenty-eight years after the war that earned it ended. And a wooden-covered scrapbook, assembled after he came home, holding the dispatches a wife cut out as they appeared and the two of them numbered together afterward — the only object here that was made rather than kept, and the one a good deal of this book was read out of.

title: The Footlocker
titleText: The Number The Footlocker
body: None of these documents agrees with all the others about exactly what happened, or exactly how many times it happened, or exactly what it should be called. Fourteen chapters into trying, this book has not resolved that disagreement either, and has stopped trying to. What it has found instead is a family that kept everything anyway — the correct figures alongside the rounded ones, the ribbon alongside the missing citation, the certain dates alongside the ones that cannot yet be checked — on the working assumption, evidently, that a thing is worth keeping whether or not anyone has yet worked out exactly what it proves.

title: The Footlocker
titleText: The Number The Footlocker
body: That is not a flaw in the record. By the end of this book, it looks very much like the record’s whole point.

title: What the Public Record Already Knew
titleText: Uncle Sam What the Public Record Already Knew
body: Sabato Rodia is not otherwise a figure in this book. His name appears once, in passing, in Angelina Calicura’s own obituary from July 1944 — “two brothers, A. Rodia of Martinez and Sam Rodia of Los Angeles” — and then not again for a decade.

title: What the Public Record Already Knew
titleText: Uncle Sam What the Public Record Already Knew
body: The public record of his life picks the thread back up on its own, independent of anything the family kept. In the summer of 1954, after thirty-three years spent building what the world would eventually call the Watts Towers, Rodia suffered a stroke. He deeded the property to a neighbor, boarded a bus, and by most published accounts never returned to Los Angeles again. Multiple independent sources — museum archives, historic-preservation records, an academic study of his life — agree on the shape of what followed: he left Watts for good in 1954, and he settled in Martinez, California, where he lived until his death in 1965.

title: What the Public Record Already Knew
titleText: Uncle Sam What the Public Record Already Knew
body: Several of those same sources state that he moved to Martinez “to be with his sister.” That detail does not survive contact with this book’s own record. Angelina had been dead ten years by 1954. The brother named in her own obituary — A. Rodia of Martinez — is the far more plausible anchor. A fact repeated across several public sources about this family is very likely a simplification, or a decade-old assumption never corrected, rather than an independently verified detail. The Calicuras had a Rodia already living in Martinez before Sabato ever arrived. That is a documented fact this book can supply that the public record of Rodia’s own life apparently could not.

title: August 1955
titleText: Uncle Sam August 1955
body: What the family’s own collection adds to this is a photograph, and the photograph carries its own date. A wall calendar hangs on the shop wall, open to August 1955 — the same month, by coincidence or not, that Calicura Bros. Meats had just finished moving into its new quarters at 700 Main Street.

title: August 1955
titleText: Uncle Sam August 1955
body: The photograph shows the shop mid-workday. Frank stands at the display case on the left, restocking it. Billy works the BIRO bandsaw on the right, a hanging carcass visible in the open cooler behind him. And in the background, behind Billy, half in shadow, stands a third man — older, watching or waiting rather than working — who the family identifies as Sabato Rodia.

title: August 1955
titleText: Uncle Sam August 1955
body: A second photograph, posed rather than caught mid-task, puts all three men together deliberately: Frank and Billy flanking Rodia, who stands at the center, visibly older than either of his nephews — the same man, seventy-six that year, who had spent three decades laying tile and glass into concrete a few hundred miles south, now standing in his sister’s hometown, in an apron, between two of her nephews.

title: August 1955
titleText: Uncle Sam August 1955
body: A third plate the family keeps of the same three is not independently the shop. Frank, his uncle, and Bill, at a table. The family names them left to right.

title: August 1955
titleText: Uncle Sam August 1955
body: Nothing in the family’s collection or the public record explains how often he came, what he did there, or whether “in the shop” meant working or simply present. Samuel Calicura’s own memory — that his great-uncle Sabato was a fixture at his father’s shop — is family testimony, corroborated by two photographs. What they confirm is narrower than the memory: in August 1955, Rodia was in Martinez, and Rodia was, at least once, standing in that shop with both of his nephews.

title: On the Record
titleText: Uncle Sam On the Record
body: What the photographs suggest, a newspaper interview confirms directly. A Martinez News-Gazette feature on a documentary being made about Rodia — undated in the collection, but referencing a film “currently being produced” and a Watts Towers preservation campaign already some years old — quotes two of his nephews and nieces by name, on the record, describing what this chapter has otherwise pieced together from photographs and family memory.

title: On the Record
titleText: Uncle Sam On the Record
body: Nick Calicura, Rodia’s nephew, told the paper plainly: “When my brothers Frank and Bill had the butcher shop, he would hang around there.” Virginia Calicura Sullivan, his niece, added texture rather than correction: “He was quite a colorful character. He was wonderful. He was warm. He loved our children.” Neither quote is new information exactly — both confirm what the August 1955 photographs already show — but both convert it from something this book infers to something two people who were there said aloud, in print, decades before this chapter existed to ask them.

title: On the Record
titleText: Uncle Sam On the Record
body: The article adds detail this book did not otherwise have. Rodia’s house in Watts burned in 1957, and the property sat untended and “slightly vandalized” from 1954 to 1958, before William Cartwright and Nicholas King purchased it in 1959 and began the preservation campaign that eventually saved it. Nick Calicura is quoted giving his uncle’s birth year as 1875, in the province of Avellino — a year the article itself calls disputed, and one that conflicts with the 1879 birth year given by the public sources already cited in this chapter. Consistent with how this book treats every other such conflict, neither figure is adopted over the other.

title: On the Record
titleText: Uncle Sam On the Record
body: The article also reports that Rodia “finished his project in the late 1940s,” which sits awkwardly beside the public record already cited here — that he worked on the towers until the stroke that ended his time in Watts altogether in 1954. Both may be true in different senses: a structure substantially complete by the late 1940s, still being maintained, tiled, and added to for years afterward.

title: Silver Spring to Martinez, 1959
titleText: Uncle Sam Silver Spring to Martinez, 1959
body: Frank Calicura’s disability claim was decided by the Veterans Administration on October 30, 1959, built on a sworn statement from an unnamed man who had served with him on an aircrew at Avon Park during September and November 1944. The same year, Jimmy Calicura’s own slide index — filled in by hand at the time, not reconstructed later — logs an entry in Section C: “Dale Ernest + Dau, ’59.” Ernest is otherwise documented in this book only through his postwar career; this is the only point where he appears inside the family’s own record, dated by the collector himself to the same year the VA closed Frank’s case.

title: Silver Spring to Martinez, 1959
titleText: Uncle Sam Silver Spring to Martinez, 1959
body: Ernest is the only member of the crew whose presence at Avon Park during the exact months the VA statement covers is independently confirmed elsewhere in this book. That he also held a Naval Ordnance Laboratory patent dated January 1959, and left for Kelsey-Hayes in Detroit that December, places a cross-country visit comfortably inside a year already documented as one of transition for him.

title: Silver Spring to Martinez, 1959
titleText: Uncle Sam Silver Spring to Martinez, 1959
body: None of this proves Ernest is the unnamed man in Frank’s claim file. What can be said is narrower, and it no longer rests on an unnamed photograph: a member of Frank’s own crew, present with him at exactly the right moment in 1944 to have witnessed what the claim describes, was also, by the family’s own contemporaneous record, in Martinez in 1959 — the same year the claim was decided. The connection is offered as likely, not documented, and stated exactly that plainly.

title: The Other Direction
titleText: Uncle Sam The Other Direction
body: Every other connection this book has drawn between the Calicura family and Sabato Rodia runs one way — Rodia coming north, into Martinez, into the family’s own shop and street. One photograph in the collection runs the other direction.

title: The Other Direction
titleText: Uncle Sam The Other Direction
body: It shows Frank Calicura and his son Samuel standing on the sidewalk outside the Watts Towers themselves, the mosaic walls and looping tower framework filling the frame behind them. Frank stands with his arms folded; Samuel, younger, stands the same way beside him. The family places the stop during a trip south to Disneyland. Samuel, born in 1952, would have been about six that year — consistent with 1958, the working date used here, a year ahead of both the Ernest visit and the VA’s decision on Frank’s claim, though nothing fixes the trip’s date itself independently of family memory; only Samuel’s birth year is separately confirmed.

title: The Other Direction
titleText: Uncle Sam The Other Direction
body: The towers were a detour on the way to or from a vacation remembered for something else entirely. Nothing in the record says what Frank told his son standing there, or whether he told him anything at all.

title: Chemnitz
titleText: Chemnitz 14 February 1945
body: First combat mission. Marshalling yard in Saxony. Copilot for the day was Richard J. Austin, on loan from John Bradley’s crew. Victor Probst flew the same morning in The Red Fox. One of 457 B-17s sent to Chemnitz while a separate force hit Dresden, forty miles away. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Key Rail City Near Capital Is Pounded

title: Cottbus
titleText: Cottbus 15 February 1945
body: Second day of the war, flown before the crew had been in combat forty-eight hours. The group lost two aircraft: Big Casino of the 335th, MACR 12378, and Easy Going of the 336th. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Osnabrück
titleText: Osnabrück 19 February 1945
body: Rail targets in the Ruhr corridor, escorted by Mustangs and Thunderbolts. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez 1,100 Heavies Hit Nazi Rails

title: Nuremberg
titleText: Nuremberg 20 February 1945
body: First of two consecutive mornings over Nuremberg. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez 900 Fortresses Rain Bombs, Incendiaries on Rail Center

title: Nuremberg
titleText: Nuremberg 21 February 1945
body: Second consecutive day at Nuremberg. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez P47s Blast Yards Near Hitler’s Den

title: Bamberg
titleText: Bamberg 22 February 1945
body: Stars and Stripes of 23 February reported six thousand aircraft against the German rail network. Bamberg is not in the story. Frank wrote it in the white margin in block capitals. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Biggest Blitz Hits Nazis

title: Bremen
titleText: Bremen 24 February 1945
body: Part of the fourteen-day run that produced 94 hours 35 minutes in February. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Munich
titleText: Munich 25 February 1945
body: Terminal rail station and marshalling yards in the city’s eastern and western districts. Fourth consecutive day the Eighth had thrown its weight against German communications. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Rail-Hitting Heavies Tear Into Munich

title: Leipzig
titleText: Leipzig 27 February 1945
body: Ninth mission in fourteen days. Air Medal awarded this date, GO 289. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Brunswick
titleText: Brunswick 3 March 1945
body: The 95th put up thirty-seven aircraft and lost one to a mid-air collision: Aunt Callie’s Baby and Paisano, both of the 335th. Nine killed. MACR 12889. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Ulm / Baumenheim
titleText: Ulm / Baumenheim 4 March 1945
body: Primary was a Messerschmitt components factory at Baumenheim; Ulm’s marshalling yard was the fallback under ten-tenths undercast. Wake at 0215. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Dortmunderfeld
titleText: Dortmunderfeld 10 March 1945
body: Industrial corridor the Eighth had been working since Chemnitz. Copilot for the day was Claude C. Greear, on loan from C.D. Crawford’s crew — the reverse of the February trade. Victor Probst flew the same morning in Poof Proof. No clipping in the scrapbook. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Swinemünde
titleText: Swinemünde 12 March 1945
body: German naval base on the Baltic, requested by Soviet command. A city swollen with civilian refugees. The crew flew it and came home. Nothing in the family’s record indicates what, if anything, Frank understood about the civilians below. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Heavies Hit Near Rhine, Along Baltic

title: Seelze
titleText: Seelze 14 March 1945
body: Among the roughest days that spring: 38 dispatched, 16 damaged, one lost, one written off after landing. The crew’s annotated captains’ chart for the day survives. Promoted to First Lieutenant the next day. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Jena
titleText: Jena 19 March 1945
body: Bombed through cloud along with Plauen. Escorts met Me 262s and Arado 234s — a jet bomber the crews had not met before. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Plane Plants, Airfields Struck By 1,200 Heavies

title: Hamburg
titleText: Hamburg 20 March 1945
body: Blohm+Voss shipyards. U-boat construction, still a priority this late in the war. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Heavies Hit U-Boat Works

title: Ahlhorn
titleText: Ahlhorn 22 March 1945
body: Luftwaffe airfield beginning to host Me 262s and Arado 234s. The crew record puts him here. The clipping kept against this page names Ingolstadt, Fürth and Grafenwöhr, not Ahlhorn. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Few Enemy Planes Up, 22 KO’d

title: Unna
titleText: Unna 23 March 1945
body: Unna–Dortmund yards, among a dozen Ruhr targets. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Ziegenhain
titleText: Ziegenhain 24 March 1945
body: No clipping survives. A number in the scrapbook and nothing else. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Hannover
titleText: Hannover 28 March 1945
body: Tank plants and a half-track factory at Hannover and Hildesheim. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez 1,250 Heavies Strike Tank, Gun Factories Near Hanover

title: Zeitz
titleText: Zeitz 31 March 1945
body: Synthetic oil plant. Recovered from a wire report, not from the family scrapbook. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Kiel
titleText: Kiel 3 April 1945
body: First of two consecutive days at Kiel. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Kiel
titleText: Kiel 4 April 1945
body: Second day. Nine bombers and four fighters lost across the Eighth; fifteen German aircraft claimed, eleven of them jets. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez Heavies Rock Kiel for 2nd Day

title: Nuremberg
titleText: Nuremberg 5 April 1945
body: Spirit of Martinez stood down for her third engine change. First of two missions in a borrowed ship. Numbered in the scrapbook the same as the rest — a record of a man, not an airplane. 44-8269 The Red Fox

title: Kaltenkirchen
titleText: Kaltenkirchen 7 April 1945
body: Second borrowed-aircraft mission. Third oak leaf cluster awarded this date, GO 720. Wilcox in the ball; Collins not aboard. Mathis as observer. 43-38942 Belligerent Beauty

title: München-Riem
titleText: München-Riem 9 April 1945
body: Back in the Spirit. Airfields around Munich believed to be bases for jet fighters. Third straight day the Eighth put more than a thousand bombers in the air. Wilcox still in the ball; Mathis still observing. Collins not on this roster. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez 1,250 Heavies Strike Munich

title: Burg
titleText: Burg 10 April 1945
body: Jet airfields in the arc around Berlin. The scrapbook names Burg among seven fields struck. Wilcox in the ball; Gearn observing. Collins not aboard. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Oranienburg
titleText: Oranienburg 20 April 1945
body: Last combat mission. Rail yards ringing Berlin. Hitler’s birthday. The scrapbook stops here. The three food drops that followed carry no number at all. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Utrecht — Lage Weide
titleText: Utrecht — Lage Weide 3 May 1945
body: Operation Chowhound. Flour, tinned meat, chocolate, powdered milk, dropped at about four hundred feet. Chowhound Three for the group. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Utrecht — Lage Weide
titleText: Utrecht — Lage Weide 5 May 1945
body: Chowhound Four. The informal truce with German flak crews still held. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Utrecht — Lage Weide
titleText: Utrecht — Lage Weide 6 May 1945
body: Chowhound Five, the day before the war in Europe ended. White bread that, to children who had lived on beet pulp, tasted like cake. 44-6838 Spirit of Martinez

title: Martinez Airport from the air

titleText: Restoring the flying field July 24, 1939. The Tribune, as the scrapbook marked it. Charles Beattie and Sam Calicura discing and dragging a runway on filled land belonging to the city. Moral support, no money. Ricks would not object to hangars and would not build them. The paper spells Beattie with two t’s. This book has used Beatie.

title: Calicura Brothers Join Aviation Cadets
titleText: Calicura Brothers Join Aviation Cadets CONTRA COSTA IN THE WAR. Dominic F. Calicura of 515 Mellus Street, accepted by the Mather Field Cadet Examining Board, to be sent to Santa Ana for pre-flight. Frank, employed with his eldest brother Sam at the Star Meat Market, standing by, expecting notice momentarily. Both Alhambra High. Joyce remaining in Martinez, employed with the Pacific Telephone and Telegraph Company. The paper names them in sequence, not as a pair.

title: Letter to a Serviceman
titleText: Letter to a Serviceman The committee to Frank, somewhere in the Eastern U.S., awaiting assignment. They heard it from a brother who also flies. An $815,000 quota already overrun; another $350,000 would buy a B-17 named City of Martinez. They asked him to put that name on his, and to let the town adopt the whole ten or eleven of you. The men painted Spirit.

title: Frank J. Calicura
titleText: Frank J. Calicura Pilot Martinez, California
body: Born 1921, son of Saverio and Angelina, one of seventeen. Learned to fly on the waterfront strip his eldest brother built. Commissioned 15 April 1944 at Turner Field. First lieutenant, serial O-828662, 335th Bomb Squadron, 95th Bomb Group. Twenty-eight combat missions, three humanitarian drops, 208 combat hours. The compilation lists thirty-one — the twenty-eight plus the food. Lt. Col. Stuart’s memorandum of 8 May 1945 certified the twenty-eight and left the drops unnumbered. Came home a first lieutenant with a commercial ticket and an instructor’s endorsement. Cut meat with his brother Bill on Main Street. Died in 1962.

title: Victor G. Probst
titleText: Victor G. Probst Copilot Yoakum, Texas
body: Right-hand seat for the tour, except three mornings: Chemnitz in The Red Fox, Ruhland in the Spirit with Getchius, Dortmunderfeld in Poof Proof. Twenty-nine with this crew. Thirty-two in the group’s compilation — a modern count, not a paper issued at Horham. His officer serial sits before Barnes’s in the same series. He is named on the Tampa order of 30 August; Barnes is not. Returned to England to study architecture at the University of London, then co-founded a Texas firm that designed hospitals, including Houston’s St. Luke’s and Texas Children’s.

title: John R. Barnes
titleText: John R. Barnes Navigator Emporium, Pennsylvania
body: Born Philadelphia, 31 January 1922, son of Leonard and Gertrude Barnes. Added to the crew at Avon Park on 6 November 1944; he is the ninth name, the one missing from the Tampa order. Thirty-one in the compilation. His officer serial follows Probst’s in the same series — commissioned second, which is why the Tampa order does not name him. Earned a doctorate at Penn State. Spent much of his career as Director of Pathology at DuPont’s Haskell Laboratory, retiring in 1982. Died 2 June 2011 in Wellsboro, Pennsylvania, age eighty-nine.

title: Marvin L. Markus
titleText: Marvin L. Markus Togglier Kingfisher, Oklahoma
body: The town already named on the wallet that would later be stamped for the crew. Flew the nose of the Spirit of Martinez. Thirty-one in the compilation. His family, seventy years later, remembered twenty-eight full bombing runs — Frank’s method, without ever seeing Frank’s paperwork. Serial 38: Eighth Service Command. Kingfisher, Oklahoma, from a source that is not the wallet. Married Dorothy Ellen O’Niel in July 1945 — sixty-nine years. Built an automotive-electric business across several towns and retired in 2003. His 2015 obituary remembered his war in a single number: twenty-eight full bombing runs. Died 30 March 2015, age eighty-nine, and was buried at Kingfisher County Memorial Cemetery with full military rites.

title: Earle F. Bogacki
titleText: Earle F. Bogacki Flight engineer / top turret Cleveland, Ohio
body: Born 1920 to Frank and Stella Bojack, a surname later changed to Bogacki — which is very likely why a contemporary wallet clipping printed “Nogacki” and still got the city right. Thirty in the compilation. One morning out: Jena, 19 March. Serial 35: Fifth Service Command. Cleveland, from a source that has nothing to do with the clipping that got his surname wrong. Stayed in uniform thirty-one years, rising to Chief Master Sergeant through Korea and Vietnam. Married Emily “Lu” McGrath on 3 May 1952. Died 14 February 2011 at ninety, buried with full military honors.

title: Robert J. Brown
titleText: Robert J. Brown Radio operator Corning, New York
body: Born 1 May 1924 to a Polish immigrant father. Radio on the Spirit from the first morning at Chemnitz. Thirty-one in the compilation. The whole tour. Serial 42: Second Service Command. Corning, New York, from a source that is not the wallet. Married in Manhattan in December 1947. The license is the last documented trace of him found.

title: Robert E. Collins
titleText: Robert E. Collins Ball turret Hutchinson, Kansas
body: Born 5 October 1923. Draft card lists the Coca-Cola Bottling Company and a boss named Lewis Scruggs. Not yet twenty when he registered. The ball turret of a B-17 became his job instead. The group’s compilation puts him in that seat from Chemnitz on, except three mornings in April: Kaltenkirchen, München-Riem, and Burg. Donald J. Wilcox flew the ball those days. Collins is back on the roster for Oranienburg, and for the food. His twenty-eight is twenty-five combat plus the three drops. Frank’s twenty-eight is combat only. Two men on the same crew, both credited with twenty-eight, and the twenty-eights are made of different missions. Neither is wrong. Serial 37: Seventh Service Command. Hutchinson, Kansas. The names are in the record. The reason he missed those three mornings is not. Signed the Hunter Field shipping ticket of 13 December 1944 in a hand consistent with the draft card. Later life is otherwise thin in the record.

title: Dale S. Ernest
titleText: Dale S. Ernest Waist gunner West Virginia
body: Present with the crew at Avon Park in the autumn of 1944 — the same window a later VA statement describes as the onset of Frank’s back injury. Thirty-one in the compilation. The whole tour. Serial 35: Fifth Service Command. West Virginia, from a source that is not the wallet. West Virginia University, then the Naval Ordnance Laboratory. By January 1959 he held a patent for an automatic depth-correcting device for moored mines. Visited Martinez that same year — “Dale Ernest + Dau, ’59,” in Jimmy Calicura’s slide index. Died in 2007.

title: James A. Titus
titleText: James A. Titus Tail gunner Lincoln, Nebraska
body: Gunnery school at Las Vegas, June 1944. Contemporary clippings from a Lincoln paper state plainly that he served in England as tail gunner on a B-17. Thirty in the compilation. One morning out: Bremen, 24 February. Serial 39: Ninth Service Command — California, Oregon, Washington, and the mountain west. Not Nebraska. The Lincoln paper and the wallet that says Omaha were writing about a young man who had already gone west. Stated, not resolved. The serial establishes where he enlisted. It does not establish where he was from. Discharged as a sergeant from Lincoln Army Air Field. Parents: Mr. and Mrs. Joe B. Titus of 3343 LaSalle Street. Later record remains thin.

title: Ellis Island
titleText: Ellis Island 1902
body: Saverio Colacurcio carries the name he was born with through Ellis Island, the Pennsylvania coal towns, and across the country to a refinery on the Carquinez Strait.

title: Colacurcio becomes Calicura
titleText: Colacurcio becomes Calicura c. 1914
body: The eldest son is eight and failing at school. The Martinez school district suggests a spelling teachers and clerks can manage. A Colacurcio in a Martinez newspaper belongs to the years before 1914. A Calicura belongs to the years after.

title: Frank James Calicura is born
titleText: Frank James Calicura is born 1921
body: One of seventeen children in the house at 515 Mellus Street. The paper supports sixteen. The family keeps seventeen.

title: Alhambra High, then the block
titleText: Alhambra High, then the block 1938
body: Yearbook: seen delivering for his brother; ambition, to swing a bat; destiny, swinging hash. He leaves 515 for 731 Mellus Street and cuts meat at the Star Meat Market.

title: Award of Merit, Treasure Island
titleText: Award of Merit, Treasure Island 1939
body: A gas-model hydroplane, judged at a fair on an artificial island built to be an airport that was never built. Outstanding junior citizen.

title: A runway in the fill
titleText: A runway in the fill 1939–1940
body: Sam Calicura Jr. and Charles Beatie drag a strip into the waterfront. In December 1940 they buy a building at the closing exposition and truck it to Martinez for a hangar.

title: The coast is grounded
titleText: The coast is grounded 8 December 1941
body: Every civil aircraft in the United States except the airliners is grounded. The ban lifts for most of the country two days later. It does not lift for the West Coast. Martinez sits on a strait with a Shell refinery above it.

title: Aviation Cadets
titleText: Aviation Cadets June 1942
body: Frank and Dominic enlist. Until January the Army had required two years of college. The requirement is struck out and replaced with an examination. Frank spends the rest of 1942 cutting meat, waiting.

title: Houghton, Michigan
titleText: Houghton, Michigan February 1943
body: College Training Detachment at a mining school on a frozen peninsula. Physics, trigonometry, snow. He leaves still undesignated.

title: First solo, Canal Field
titleText: First solo, Canal Field 19 October 1943
body: Greenville Aviation School, Ocala. Signed off by Ellis G. Ort. The certificate is a cartoon: Woody Woodpecker, not an eagle.

title: Wings, bars, instruments
titleText: Wings, bars, instruments 15 April 1944
body: Turner Field, Class 44-D. Commission, instrument qualification, and pilot rating land on the same date. A tornado grounds the field that midnight.

title: Frank James Calicura Jr.
titleText: Frank James Calicura Jr. 20 June 1944
body: Born 3:15 p.m. at Community Hospital, Martinez, seven pounds seven ounces. The Gazette: “New ‘General’ at Lieut. Calicura Home.” Frank is at Hendricks Field and has not yet seen him.

title: Angelina dies
titleText: Angelina dies 21 July 1944
body: After an illness of two days, at fifty-eight. Pioneer Mother Dies. Frank is home on leave from Hendricks. He holds a one-month-old son, then goes back.

title: A will at Avon Park
titleText: A will at Avon Park 7 September 1944
body: Second lieutenant O-828662 names Joyce B. Calicura of 731 Mellus Street executrix. He has not yet flown a combat mission.

title: Shipment FQ-555-CA
titleText: Shipment FQ-555-CA 18 December 1944
body: Nine signatures on a shipping ticket at Grenier Field. They ferry B-17G 44-6830, not the Spirit — an aircraft built eight serials away, in the same shed, the same month.

title: Station 119
titleText: Station 119 6 January 1945
body: Arrival in the European theater, 95th Bomb Group, Horham, Suffolk. Formal assignment to the 335th a few days later.

title: Eight empty places
titleText: Eight empty places 3 February 1945
body: A thousand B-17s to Berlin. Eight aircraft of the 95th do not come home. Frank’s crew is not yet in rotation. He is in the same huts.

title: Mission one: Chemnitz
titleText: Mission one: Chemnitz 14 February 1945
body: The name goes up on the board. Not Dresden — a rail yard forty miles away, the same morning.

title: Spirit of Martinez
titleText: Spirit of Martinez Spring 1945
body: The city doubles its Sixth War Loan quota. 44-6838 is christened after the fact. The crew has already been flying her under the name. “We can brag about her, Ray. Not once did we have to turn back.”

title: Oranienburg
titleText: Oranienburg 20 April 1945
body: The twenty-eighth and last combat mission. The scrapbook stops. The food drops that follow carry no number.

title: Utrecht, three mornings
titleText: Utrecht, three mornings 3–6 May 1945
body: Operation Chowhound. Flour and chocolate at four hundred feet over Lage Weide. The Germans, for the most part, keep their word.

title: Bradley Field
titleText: Bradley Field 21 June 1945
body: The Spirit lands in Connecticut. Before he gets his things off, they dismantle her and tow her away. Sold for scrap at Kingman on 19 December.

title: Relief from active duty
titleText: Relief from active duty 12 November 1945
body: First Lieutenant, Air Corps. MOS: Pilot (1091). Civilian occupation: butcher and meatcutter. Processed at March Field, California.

title: Sam Calicura Jr. dies
titleText: Sam Calicura Jr. dies 2 March 1946
body: Thirty-nine or forty. He has just reopened the Martinez Airport with Charlie Beatie and his three brothers. He built the field, watched the war take it, and lived long enough to run it again.

title: Joyce’s credentials
titleText: Joyce’s credentials 1948
body: Deputy Sheriff of Contra Costa County, badge 72, and a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit. Frank renews his Second Class Airmen medical with no limitations.

title: 700 Main Street
titleText: 700 Main Street August 1955
body: Frank and Bill leave Martellacci’s for their own renovated shop. In the same month a wall calendar dates a photograph: Sabato Rodia standing between his nephews in the meat market.

title: The claim is denied
titleText: The claim is denied 30 October 1959
body: Claim C-1,302,621. A back that needed help getting into an airplane in 1944 is found either not service-connected, or service-connected but below ten percent. Both readings live in the same sentence.

title: Provenance
titleText: Provenance
body: This account was assembled from four kinds of material, and the difference between them matters more than any individual fact drawn from any of them.

title: Provenance
titleText: Provenance
body: It was assembled by a descendant. Frank Calicura was this writer’s grandfather, Joyce Calicura his grandmother, and Samuel Calicura — cited as a family witness, and the boy standing beside his father in the photograph that closes the book — is this writer’s father. The relationship is stated here because the same standard is applied to every other source in these pages: the reader is told who supplied a piece of evidence, and how close to it they stood.

title: The reading
titleText: The reading
body: The voice that follows each chapter is synthetic. It is a reading of the text as written, not a recording.

title: The family collection
titleText: The family collection
body: Military records, certificates, photographs, correspondence, newspaper clippings, and physical artifacts held by the descendants of Saverio and Angelina Calicura of Martinez, California.

title: The family collection
titleText: The family collection
body: It is not catalogued, not complete, and not neutral. It preserves what a family chose to keep, which is a different thing from what happened. One of those objects is a copy of Contrails, the 95th Bomb Group yearbook of 1945, from which the nose-art montage in the archive is taken.

title: The institutional record
titleText: The institutional record
body: Unit histories, crew records, mission logs, government correspondence, and the surviving federal paperwork of a man’s service. This material is more systematic and no more complete.

title: The institutional record
titleText: The institutional record
body: A great deal of it burned in St. Louis in 1973.

title: The institutional record
titleText: The institutional record
body: The 95th Bomb Group’s compiled crew record for this crew is published at 95thbgdb.com/crew/59. It is a modern database, not a paper issued at Horham. Each sortie on the mission board links to that compilation’s corresponding mission page. Each man on the roster links to its corresponding person page. The same compilation credits Victor G. Probst with thirty-two sorties — twenty-nine with this crew, three on loan. That figure appears on his person page and in no wartime document held by this family.

title: The institutional record
titleText: The institutional record
body: The Eighth Air Force daily mission record is compiled at americanarchive.iwm.org.uk. It is a modern finding aid, not a paper issued at Horham. Combat sorties on the mission board link to that compilation’s corresponding day page. The three food drops do not: Chowhound is not in the combat-mission series, and the archive’s Chowhound page is dated 2 May, not the days this crew flew.

title: The institutional record
titleText: The institutional record
body: The same archive holds a person page for John R. Barnes at americanarchive.iwm.org.uk/archive/person/john-r-barnes — the other copy is americanairmuseum.com/person/127516 — that identifies him as navigator of the Spirit of Martinez. It is a modern compilation, not a paper issued at Horham. The biography on that page was supplied in part by his son.

title: The institutional record
titleText: The institutional record
body: Dave Osborne’s B-17 Fortress Master Log, which that archive also draws on, lists 44-6838 as CAL'S RASCALS aka THE SPIRIT OF MARTINEZ. That is the log’s other name for the serial, not a second christening.

title: The contemporary press
titleText: The contemporary press
body: Wire reports and hometown papers, several of them clipped and annotated by hand at the time. A substantial share of the mission clippings cited here comes from a single object: the scrapbook Joyce Calicura kept through the war and for the rest of her life.

title: The contemporary press
titleText: The contemporary press
body: She clipped the dispatches as they appeared. After Frank came home the two of them sequenced and numbered them together, glued to black pages and bound in a wooden cover made for the purpose.

title: The contemporary press
titleText: The contemporary press
body: The war coverage reproduced here is not a neutral sample of what the papers printed. It is what one woman in Martinez chose to cut out and keep while her husband was flying, arranged afterward in the order the missions were flown. Newspaper content is referenced by headline, publication, and date, paraphrased rather than reproduced, and treated throughout as what it is: a first draft written under deadline by people who did not have access to the records now available.

title: The contemporary press
titleText: The contemporary press
body: Later obituaries are a different thing from the wartime clippings. Marvin L. Markus’s 2015 notice in the Bartlesville Examiner-Enterprise is kept at okcemeteries.net/kingfisher/kingfisher/m/markusmlobit.htm, with a shorter funeral-home listing at stumpff.org. Emily “Lu” Bogacki’s 2020 notice is at wkbn.com/my-valley-tributes/emily-lu-bogacki-greenville-pa/. They are what those families told a paper after the men were gone. They are cited as such.

title: The mission charts
titleText: The mission charts
body: Fourteen printed aeronautical charts, Newcastle to Prague, heights in feet, each headed CAPTAINS OF AIRCRAFT MAP and each annotated by hand with a mission number, a date, control points and their times, an initial point, a rally point, and flak concentrations shaded in colored pencil. They cover missions one through fourteen without a gap.

title: The mission charts
titleText: The mission charts
body: Whose hand made the annotations is not established here.

title: The mission charts
titleText: The mission charts
body: What the charts record is a mission count kept while the tour was still being flown. Where that count can be checked against the group’s crew record — at missions three, four, five, six, eight, nine, ten, twelve, thirteen and fourteen — the two agree.

title: The mission charts
titleText: The mission charts
body: The flak shading is planned intelligence, not observation. The times are briefed times, not flown times.

title: Disagreements are stated, not resolved
titleText: Disagreements are stated, not resolved
body: Where the three records conflict, the conflict is named on the page. Nothing is quietly reconciled to make a cleaner story.

title: Inferences are labelled where they are made
titleText: Inferences are labelled where they are made
body: Where a claim rests on inference rather than a document, it is identified as an inference in the text itself rather than buried in a note at the back.

title: Absence is reported
titleText: Absence is reported
body: Gaps in the record are stated as gaps. Nothing has been supplied to fill them.

title: The clipping is not the event
titleText: The clipping is not the event
body: A newspaper is evidence of what a paper printed, on deadline, at a distance. It is not evidence of what happened.

title: A note on sources
titleText: A note on sources
body: None of these documents agrees with all the others about exactly what happened, or exactly how many times it happened. The book stopped trying to resolve that. A family kept everything anyway.
